### 6.4 The McGucken construction of the Hilbert space 𝓗 (Theorem 6.1): 𝓗 as the unique irreducible separable Hilbert-space representation of the Weyl form of the McGucken-derived canonical commutator algebra, via Stone-von Neumann uniqueness

The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework derives the Hilbert space through two complementary routes: a **dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel** wavefront-geometric derivation via McGucken-Sphere overlap on the spatial slice (§6.4.5), and a **Algebraic Channel** algebraic derivation via the McGucken-derived canonical commutator algebra and Stone–von Neumann uniqueness (present subsection). Both routes start from the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic; both reach the same Hilbert space 𝓗 ≅ L²(ℝ³, d³x); they operate through derivationally distinct mechanisms — dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel on wavefront geometry, Algebraic Channel on operator algebra — and converge on the same result. The present subsection develops Algebraic Channel in six steps; §6.4.5 develops dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel in six steps; §6.4.6 displays the convergence in tabular form. (The dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel is the foundational channel of the **McGucken Duality** carrying the full +ic-oriented Sphere expansion; the Algebraic Channel is the T-invariant projection ΠA of the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel; both descend from dx₄/dt = ic and are catalogued in §16’s projection-theorem reading.)

#### 6.4.1 Algebraic Channel architecture

The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework derives the Hilbert space as the *forced* representation space of the canonical commutator algebra established in Theorem 5.1. The construction proceeds in six steps: (1) the upstream geometric setup of the McGucken source space; (2) the Lorentzian constraint surface as derived spacetime; (3) the Frobenius selection of ℂ from one perpendicular axis; (4) the canonical commutator algebra derived from x₄-perpendicularity through Theorem 5.1; (5) passage to the Weyl form to circumvent domain issues from unbounded operators; (6) the Stone–von Neumann uniqueness theorem identifying the Hilbert space as the unique irreducible separable representation. No external Riesz–Fischer L² completion is invoked as foundational input. The Hilbert space emerges as forced by the McGucken-derived commutator algebra through Stone–von Neumann uniqueness — Algebraic Channel McGucken machinery driving the derivation, with the upstream input being the geometric perpendicularity of x₄ and the action quantization of x₄-advance, both descending from dx₄/dt = ic.

*The Algebraic Channel’s foundational dependence on the McGucken Sphere.* The Algebraic Channel construction below operates through operator algebra and representation theory — the canonical commutator $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$, the Weyl form $U(a)V(b) = \exp(-ia \cdot b/\hbar)V(b)U(a)$, and Stone–von Neumann uniqueness as the input-output structure that forces the Hilbert space. The surface presentation may suggest that the Algebraic Channel is “purely algebraic” in contrast to the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel’s “wavefront-geometric” route through Huygens superposition. **This reading is incorrect.** The Algebraic Channel rests on the McGucken Sphere through Theorem 5.1, which derives the canonical commutator from Sphere geometry: the imaginary unit $i$ in the non-closure quantum $i\hbar$ is the algebraic marker for the Sphere’s $x_4$-perpendicularity (Theorem 3.1, with Frobenius selection of $\mathbb{C}$ from one perpendicular axis in §4.1), and the action quantum $\hbar$ is the action accumulated per Planck-frequency oscillation along any radial direction of the Sphere (Proposition 2.2). The product $i\hbar$ in the canonical commutator is therefore the operator-level algebraic record of the Sphere’s two intrinsic constants — perpendicularity and action quantization — joined by Proposition 12.10’s reading of the CCR as the operator-level expression of the Sphere’s geometric perpendicularity $x_1 x_2 x_3 \perp x_4$.

The Algebraic Channel is therefore **Sphere-grounded** at its algebraic foundation. Stripping the Sphere from the Algebraic Channel collapses Theorem 5.1’s derivation of the CCR (no Sphere → no x₄-perpendicularity → no $i$ in $i\hbar$; no Sphere → no x₄-advance oscillation → no $\hbar$ in $i\hbar$), which in turn collapses the Weyl algebra and the input to Stone–von Neumann, which collapses the unique-representation conclusion. The Algebraic Channel is best understood as the **algebraic presentation of Sphere geometry**: operator algebra is what the Sphere’s geometry looks like at the operator-algebra cascade level, just as Huygens–Fresnel–Kirchhoff superposition is what the same Sphere’s geometry looks like at the wavefront cascade level. Both channels rest on the same Sphere; they differ only in which cascade level of structure they make explicit. By the projection-theorem reading of §16 (the McGucken Duality), the Algebraic Channel is the $T$-invariant projection $\Pi_A$ of the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel — the algebraic shadow of the Sphere’s full $+ic$-oriented geometry, with the $+ic$ orientation projected away and the algebraic structure surviving.

By the Space-Operator Cogeneration Theorem (Theorem 2.4), the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic generates 𝓜_G = (E₄, Φ_M, D_M, Σ_M): the ambient four-dimensional space, the constraint Φ_M = x₄ - ict, the source operator D_M = ∂\_t + ic ∂\_x₄, and the McGucken measure Σ_M. All four components descend from the single principle.

By Lemma 2.5, the constraint surface Φ_M⁻¹(0), equipped with the metric induced from the four-dimensional Euclidean line element, is the Lorentzian spacetime Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ with signature (−,+,+,+). The Lorentzian signature descends directly from (ict)² = −c² t² — the squared form of dx₄/dt = ic.

By Theorem 3.1, scalar amplitudes ψ on Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ are ℂ-valued because the integrated form x₄ = ict introduces the imaginary unit i as the algebraic marker for x₄’s perpendicularity to x₁x₂x₃. The Frobenius theorem on associative real division algebras (Frobenius 1877 \[52\]) admits exactly three options:

-   ℝ: zero independent imaginary units (zero perpendicular axes beyond x₁x₂x₃);
-   ℂ: one independent imaginary unit i with i² = −1 (one perpendicular axis);
-   ℍ: three independent imaginary units i, j, k with i² = j² = k² = ijk = −1 (three perpendicular axes).

The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework specifies exactly one fourth dimension x₄ perpendicular to x₁x₂x₃. One perpendicular axis. One imaginary unit. Frobenius then forces ℂ as the unique division algebra. Had the McGucken Principle asserted three perpendicular dimensions with quaternion algebra, the dx₄/dt = ic framework would have produced ℍ (quaternionic QM, empirically excluded by Renou et al. 2021 \[183\]). Had it asserted no perpendicular dimension, the dx₄/dt = ic framework would have produced ℝ (the Euclidean shadow obtained by Wick-rotating away the i). The seventy-year ℝ/ℂ/ℍ ambiguity in the prior tradition (Piron 1964 \[27\], Solèr 1995 \[28\], Jordan–von Neumann–Wigner 1934 \[21\]) vanishes once perpendicular dimensionality is part of the foundational statement.

The complex linear space of McGucken amplitudes is

𝓥 = { ψ : Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ → ℂ }

under pointwise addition and ℂ-scalar multiplication. 𝓥 is a complex vector space — not yet a Hilbert space, not yet equipped with an inner product. The Hilbert-space structure is supplied in steps 4–6 by the canonical commutator algebra acting on 𝓥, not by writing down an inner-product formula by hand.

By Theorem 5.1 of the present paper, the canonical commutator

\[q̂\_i, p̂\_j\] = iℏ δ\_{ij} 𝟙, \[q̂\_i, q̂\_j\] = 0, \[p̂\_i, p̂\_j\] = 0, i, j ∈ {1, 2, 3},

descends from dx₄/dt = ic through two channels: (i) the imaginary unit i is the perpendicularity marker for x₄ ⊥ x₁x₂x₃, inherited from the integrated form x₄ = ict (Theorem 3.1), and (ii) the action quantum ℏ is the action-per-oscillation of x₄-advance at the Planck frequency (Proposition 2.2). The product iℏ on the right-hand side is therefore the conjunction of perpendicularity and action quantization — the McGucken Principle in operator form, expressed as the non-closure of the canonical commutator.

The algebra generated by {q̂\_i, p̂\_i, 𝟙 : i = 1, 2, 3} together with these relations is the **three-dimensional Heisenberg algebra** $\mathfrak{h}_3$ over ℂ. This algebra is the McGucken-derived structure that the Hilbert space must carry as an irreducible representation.

The operators $\hat{q}_i$ and $\hat{p}_j$ cannot both be bounded on any Hilbert space carrying the representation $[\hat{q}_i, \hat{p}_j] = i\hbar \delta_{ij}\, \mathbb{1}$. This is the **Wielandt–Wintner theorem** (Wielandt, *Mathematische Annalen* 121, 21–24, 1949; Wintner, *Physical Review* 71, 738, 1947): if $[A, B] = c\, \mathbb{1}$ with $c \neq 0$ on a Banach algebra, then no realization of $A, B$ as bounded operators exists. Domain issues from unbounded operators then obstruct a direct uniqueness statement at the level of $\hat{q}, \hat{p}$ themselves.

The standard resolution, introduced by Weyl in 1928 (*Gruppentheorie und Quantenmechanik* \[184\]), is to pass to the exponentiated form. Define the **Weyl unitaries**

$$U(a) := \exp(i a \cdot \hat{q} / \hbar), \quad V(b) := \exp(i b \cdot \hat{p} / \hbar), \quad a, b \in \mathbb{R}^3.$$

The required self-adjointness of $\hat{q}, \hat{p}$ is established on the McGucken-derived Schwartz domain $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3) \subset \mathcal{V}$ — the natural domain of Sphere wavefunctions with rapid decay, which arises naturally as finite Sphere superpositions with Gaussian source-event distributions (cf. Lemma 6.1.6 of §6.4.5). Both $\hat{q}_i$ (multiplication by $x_i$) and $\hat{p}_i = -i\hbar\, \partial/\partial x_i$ are formally Hermitian on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ with vanishing deficiency indices $n_\pm = \dim \ker(T^* \mp i) = 0$ (Reed–Simon I, §VIII.2–VIII.3), hence essentially self-adjoint with unique self-adjoint closures. Stone’s theorem (1930) \[108\] then guarantees that the one-parameter unitary families $\exp(i a \cdot \hat{q}/\hbar)$ and $\exp(i b \cdot \hat{p}/\hbar)$ generated by these self-adjoint operators are strongly continuous and bounded on the closure of $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ — that is, $U(a)$ and $V(b)$ are bounded unitary operators with full domain.

The Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula applied to $e^X e^Y$ with $X = i a \cdot \hat{q}/\hbar$ and $Y = i b \cdot \hat{p}/\hbar$ has commutator
$$[X, Y] = (i/\hbar)^2\, [a \cdot \hat{q}, b \cdot \hat{p}] = (i/\hbar)^2 \cdot i\hbar\, (a \cdot b)\, \mathbb{1} = -i\, (a \cdot b)/\hbar \cdot \mathbb{1},$$
a c-number multiple of the identity — a *central* element of the Heisenberg algebra $\mathfrak{h}_3$ that commutes with both $X$ and $Y$. All higher-order nested commutators $[X, [X, Y]] = [Y, [X, Y]] = \cdots = 0$ vanish identically because $[X, Y]$ commutes with everything. The BCH series therefore **truncates exactly at the first commutator**: $e^X e^Y = e^{X + Y + [X,Y]/2}$ and $e^Y e^X = e^{X + Y - [X,Y]/2}$, so $e^X e^Y = e^{[X,Y]}\, e^Y e^X$. This yields the **Weyl form of the canonical commutation relation** exactly (not merely formally):

$$U(a)\, V(b) = \exp\!\big(-i\, (a \cdot b)/\hbar\big)\, V(b)\, U(a), \quad a, b \in \mathbb{R}^3.$$

This is the McGucken-derived statement at the bounded-operator level: $U(a)$ and $V(b)$ are two strongly continuous unitary representations of $(\mathbb{R}^3, +)$ on whatever Hilbert space carries the representation, failing to commute by exactly the phase $\exp(-i a \cdot b / \hbar)$. The phase contains both McGucken constants of the Principle: $i$ from $x_4$-perpendicularity (Theorem 3.1) and $\hbar$ from action quantization (Proposition 2.2), with $i\hbar$ identified as the operator-level non-closure quantum of the McGucken Sphere’s $x_1 x_2 x_3 \perp x_4$ geometric perpendicularity (Proposition 12.10).

With the McGucken-derived Weyl algebra in place, the Hilbert space is forced by a uniqueness theorem:

**Theorem (Stone 1930 \[108\]; von Neumann 1931 \[109\]).** *Let* U(a), V(b), a, b ∈ ℝ\^n *be a pair of strongly continuous unitary representations of the additive group* (ℝ\^n, +) *on a separable complex Hilbert space* 𝓗, *satisfying the Weyl relation*

U(a) V(b) = exp(-i (a · b)/ℏ) V(b) U(a).

*Assume the representation is irreducible: no proper closed subspace of* 𝓗 *is invariant under all* U(a) *and* V(b). *Then the representation is unitarily equivalent to the* **Schrödinger representation** *on* L²(ℝ\^n, d\^n x):

(U(a) ψ)(x) = exp(i (a · x)/ℏ) ψ(x), (V(b) ψ)(x) = ψ(x + b).

*The unitary equivalence is unique up to multiplication by a complex scalar of modulus 1.*

The Stone–von Neumann theorem is a mathematical fact about the irreducible unitary representations of the Heisenberg group; the proof is in Folland’s *Harmonic Analysis in Phase Space* (Princeton 1989, Theorem 1.50) or Reed–Simon I, Theorem VIII.14. The theorem requires three inputs: (a) the Weyl relation with constant ℏ ≠ 0, (b) strong continuity of U(·) and V(·), (c) separability and irreducibility of the representation.

**Verification of the three inputs from the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework.**

*(a) The Weyl relation* with constant iℏ is supplied by Step 5, with the constant ℏ ≠ 0 supplied by Proposition 2.2’s action-quantization clause (a nonzero quantum of action per Planck-frequency oscillation of x₄-advance — empirically ℏ ≈ 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, by Planck’s 1900 black-body constant).

*(b) Strong continuity* of the unitary families $U(a), V(b)$ in their parameters $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is established as follows. The operators $\hat{q}_i$ (multiplication by spatial coordinate $x_i$) and $\hat{p}_i = -i\hbar\, \partial/\partial x_i$ supplied by Theorem 5.1 are formally Hermitian on the Schwartz space $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ — the natural McGucken-derived domain of rapidly decaying Sphere-wavefunction superpositions. Their **deficiency indices** $n_\pm(T) := \dim \ker(T^* \mp i)$ both vanish: $n_+(\hat{q}_i) = n_-(\hat{q}_i) = 0$ follows from the spectral character of multiplication-by-coordinate (continuous spectrum on $\mathbb{R}$, with no $\pm i$ in the spectrum); $n_+(\hat{p}_i) = n_-(\hat{p}_i) = 0$ follows analogously via the unitary Fourier transform (Reed–Simon I, §VIII.3), which intertwines $\hat{p}_i$ with multiplication-by-momentum on the momentum-representation Hilbert space. With $n_+ = n_- = 0$, both $\hat{q}_i$ and $\hat{p}_i$ are **essentially self-adjoint** on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ by the deficiency-index criterion (Reed–Simon II, Theorem X.1) — each admits a unique self-adjoint extension to its respective closure. Stone’s theorem (1930) \[108\] then guarantees that the one-parameter unitary family $U(a) = \exp(i a \cdot \hat{q}/\hbar)$ generated by the self-adjoint $\hat{q}$ is strongly continuous in $a$, and likewise $V(b) = \exp(i b \cdot \hat{p}/\hbar)$ is strongly continuous in $b$. The McGucken-derived domain $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ — itself a consequence of $\mathrm{dx}_4/\mathrm{dt} = ic$ via the Schwartz-class decay of Sphere-wavefunction Gaussian source distributions (Lemma 6.1.6) — supplies the precise functional-analytic content needed for the deficiency-index criterion to apply.

*(c) Irreducibility* of the McGucken representation is established by the geometry of the dx₄/dt = ic framework. The spatial slice $\mathbb{R}^3$ on which the Weyl unitaries act is itself the spatial slice of the McGucken-derived Lorentzian spacetime Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ at fixed parameter time $t$ (the constraint surface $\Phi_M = 0$ of Lemma 2.5 restricted to fixed $x_4 = ict$). The translation group $(\mathbb{R}^3, +)$ generating $V(b)$ is the spatial-translation subgroup of the isometry group of Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ — a Killing-vector subgroup of the McGucken-derived Lorentzian metric, forced by the spatial homogeneity of the McGucken-Sphere construction (every event of Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ is a permissible source event with its own Sphere, by the universality clause of $\mathrm{dx}_4/\mathrm{dt} = ic$). The modulation group $(\mathbb{R}^3, +)$ generating $U(a)$ is the Fourier dual — the momentum-translation subgroup acting on the spatial-slice Fourier representation. The Weyl unitaries therefore act on $\mathcal{V}$ (the space of complex amplitudes from Step 3) by translation ($V(b)$) and modulation ($U(a)$), both representing physical symmetries of the McGucken-Sphere construction inherited from $\mathrm{dx}_4/\mathrm{dt} = ic$.

An invariant closed subspace $\mathcal{W} \subsetneq \mathcal{V}$ would need to be closed under both translations $V(b)$ for all $b \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and modulations $U(a)$ for all $a \in \mathbb{R}^3$. By the Wiener tauberian theorem (Wiener 1932; or directly: the joint action of all translations and all modulations on $L^2$ is well-known to be irreducible, see Folland 1989 §1.5), no nontrivial closed subspace of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is preserved by all translations and all modulations simultaneously. The same applies to the McGucken amplitude space $\mathcal{V}$ by the Frobenius identification of $\mathbb{C}$-valued fields on $\mathbb{R}^3$ (Step 3) with $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$-type amplitudes — the joint translation–modulation action is irreducible on any candidate complete representation. *Separability* follows because the orbit of any single normalized $\psi_0 \in \mathcal{V}$ under $\{U(a) V(b) : a, b \in \mathbb{Q}^3\}$ is a countable dense subset in the strong topology, with $\mathbb{Q}^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ being a countable dense subgroup of the spatial slice supplied by the second-countability of the McGucken-derived spatial-slice topology.

All three inputs of Stone–von Neumann are McGucken-supplied: (a) from Theorem 5.1 + Proposition 2.2, (b) from Theorem 5.1’s self-adjointness + Stone 1930, (c) from the geometry of x₄-perpendicular translations and modulations acting on the spatial slice ℝ³.

**Theorem 6.1 (Hilbert space from dx₄/dt = ic).** *The Hilbert space* 𝓗 *of nonrelativistic single-particle quantum mechanics is the unique irreducible separable Hilbert-space representation of the Weyl form of the McGucken-derived canonical commutator algebra:*

U(a) V(b) = exp(-i (a · b)/ℏ) V(b) U(a), a, b ∈ ℝ³,

*with* iℏ *supplied by Theorem 5.1 (i from x₄-perpendicularity, Theorem 3.1; ℏ from action quantization, Proposition 2.2). By the Stone–von Neumann uniqueness theorem (Stone 1930 \[108\]; von Neumann 1931 \[109\]), this representation is unitarily equivalent to the Schrödinger representation on* L²(ℝ³, d³x):

$𝓗 ≅ L²(ℝ³, d³x),$

*with the Weyl unitaries acting as*

(U(a) ψ)(x) = exp(i (a · x)/ℏ) ψ(x), (V(b) ψ)(x) = ψ(x + b).

**Lemma 6.1.6 (Hermite functions from Gaussian source-event distributions on McGucken Spheres; density in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3x)$).** *Let $\mathcal{V} = \mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{C}}\{\psi_E(\cdot, t) : E \in \mathbb{M}_{1,3}\}$ denote the pre-Hilbert space of finite $\mathbb{C}$-linear combinations of McGucken-Sphere wavefronts at parameter time $t > 0$ (Step 2 of §6.4.5), equipped with the geometric overlap inner product $\langle \varphi, \psi \rangle_t = \int \varphi^*\psi\, d^3x$ (Step 3). Then:*

*(i) The Cauchy completion of $(\mathcal{V}, \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_t)$ in the norm topology $\|\psi\|_t = \sqrt{\langle\psi,\psi\rangle_t}$ equals $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3x)$.*

*(ii) The Hermite functions $h_n(x) = H_n(x) \exp(-x^2/2)$, where $H_n$ are the (physicists’) Hermite polynomials, form an explicit complete orthonormal basis of the Cauchy completion. Each $h_n$ arises as a Cauchy limit of finite $\mathbb{C}$-linear combinations of McGucken-Sphere wavefronts with Gaussian source-event distributions and polynomial weighting.*

**Proof.**

*Step A (Gaussian wavepackets as Cauchy limits of finite Sphere superpositions).* For each width $\sigma > 0$, define the Gaussian source-event distribution
$$g_\sigma(x_E) := (\pi\sigma^2)^{-3/4} \exp\!\big(-|x_E|^2/(2\sigma^2)\big) \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3).$$
The McGucken-Sphere wavefront generated by source distribution $g_\sigma$ at proper time $\tau = 0$, propagated forward to parameter time $t > 0$ by Sphere expansion, is the continuous superposition
$$\psi_{g_\sigma}(x, t) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} g_\sigma(x_E)\, \psi_{x_E}(x, t)\, d^3 x_E,$$
where $\psi_{x_E}(\cdot, t)$ is the McGucken-Sphere wavefront from a source event at spatial position $x_E$. By Theorem 9.0.5 of §9.2.5 (itself a theorem of $\mathrm{dx}_4/\mathrm{dt} = ic$ — the nonrelativistic Sphere wavefront’s envelope dynamics is shown there to be the free Schrödinger evolution via the McGucken-Sphere mass-shell constraint and Compton-frequency oscillation, see §9.2.5 Steps 1–7), this continuous Sphere superposition equals the free Schrödinger evolution of the initial distribution:
$$\psi_{g_\sigma}(x, t) = (U_{\text{free}}(t)\, g_\sigma)(x),$$
where $U_{\text{free}}(t) = \exp(-it H_{\text{free}}/\hbar)$ is the free-particle unitary evolution operator on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$. Since $g_\sigma \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ and $U_{\text{free}}(t)$ is unitary on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ (Theorem 9.2: unitarity from $x_4$-flux conservation), $\psi_{g_\sigma}(\cdot, t) \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$.

Approximating the continuous Gaussian source distribution $g_\sigma\, d^3 x_E$ by finite Riemann sums of point masses: for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\{x_{E_{n,k}}\}_{k=1}^{N_n}$ be a grid of source-event positions with mesh size $\delta_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, and set $c_{n,k} := g_\sigma(x_{E_{n,k}})\, \delta_n^3$. The corresponding finite Sphere superposition is
$$\psi_n(x, t) := \sum_{k=1}^{N_n} c_{n,k}\, \psi_{x_{E_{n,k}}}(x, t) \in \mathcal{V}.$$
By translation invariance of the McGucken-Sphere construction and the $L^2$-continuity of the propagator action $g \mapsto U_{\text{free}}(t)\, g$ in the source distribution $g$, the sequence $\{\psi_n(\cdot, t)\}$ converges in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ to $\psi_{g_\sigma}(\cdot, t)$ as $n \to \infty$. (The integrand $g_\sigma(x_E) \psi_{x_E}(\cdot, t)$ is $L^2$-continuous in $x_E$ by translation invariance — the Sphere wavefront from a translated source is the spatial translate of the Sphere wavefront from the origin — and the Gaussian decay of $g_\sigma$ supplies an $L^1$-dominating function for the Riemann-sum convergence on the source-event integration.) Therefore $\psi_{g_\sigma}(\cdot, t)$ lies in the $L^2$-Cauchy completion of $\mathcal{V}$.

At a reference parameter time $t_0$ chosen so that the free-Schrödinger phase $\exp(-i\hbar t_0 |k|^2/(2m))$ combines with the source-distribution Gaussian Fourier transform $\exp(-\sigma^2 |k|^2/2)$ to give the standard Hermite ground-state Fourier transform, $\psi_{g_{\sigma_0}}(\cdot, t_0) = h_0$ up to normalization (with $\sigma_0$ chosen so the combined complex width equals 1, giving $h_0(x) = \pi^{-3/4} \exp(-|x|^2/2)$). The Hermite ground state $h_0$ is therefore in the $L^2$-Cauchy completion of finite Sphere superpositions.

*Step B (Higher Hermite functions via creation-operator action).* The Hermite functions satisfy the recursion
$$h_{n+1}(x) = a^\dagger\, h_n(x)\, /\sqrt{n+1}, \qquad a^\dagger := (x - d/dx)/\sqrt{2}.$$
The position multiplication operator $x$ and the spatial derivative operator $d/dx$ are both expressible as Cauchy limits of finite source-position operations on Sphere superpositions:

-   *Position multiplication $x$.* By translation invariance of the McGucken-Sphere construction — itself the universality clause of $\mathrm{dx}_4/\mathrm{dt} = ic$ formalized as Theorem 2.4 clause (iv), where the wavefront assignment $\Sigma_M : p \mapsto \Sigma^+(p)$ is translation-invariant by the universality of the McGucken Principle across all events of Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ — the wavefront from a translated source satisfies $\psi_{x_E}(x, t) = \psi_0(x - x_E, t)$, where $\psi_0$ denotes the wavefront from a source at the origin. Differentiating both sides in $x_E$ at $x_E = 0$ and inverting gives the spatial-coordinate representation of position multiplication as a finite-difference limit of source-position-translated Sphere wavefronts: $x \cdot \psi_0(x, t) = -\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon^{-1}[\psi_{\varepsilon \hat{x}}(x, t) - \psi_0(x, t)]$ componentwise (where $\hat{x}$ is a spatial unit vector in the relevant direction; higher coordinate components follow by symmetry). Position multiplication on any Sphere superposition is therefore a Cauchy limit of finite Sphere superpositions with translated source events.

-   *Spatial derivative $d/dx$.* Directly from the translation identity, $\partial_x \psi_0(x, t) = -\partial_{x_E} \psi_{x_E}(x, t)\big|_{x_E = 0}$. Finite differences $\bigl(\psi_{x_E + \varepsilon \hat{x}}(x, t) - \psi_{x_E}(x, t)\bigr)/\varepsilon$ converge to $-\partial_{x} \psi_0(x, t)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Spatial differentiation on any Sphere superposition is therefore a Cauchy limit of finite Sphere superpositions with infinitesimally-translated source events.

Both operations preserve the $L^2$-Cauchy completion. Applying the creation operator $a^\dagger = (x - d/dx)/\sqrt{2}$ to $h_0$ (in the completion by Step A) gives $h_1$, also in the completion. Inductively, every $h_n = (a^\dagger)^n h_0 / \sqrt{n!}$ is a Cauchy limit of finite Sphere superpositions.

*Step C (Density via the Hermite basis).* The three-dimensional Hermite functions $\{h_{n_1}(x_1)\, h_{n_2}(x_2)\, h_{n_3}(x_3) : (n_1, n_2, n_3) \in \mathbb{N}^3\}$ form a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3x)$ (Reed–Simon I, *Methods of Modern Mathematical Physics: Functional Analysis*, Theorem V.7, applied componentwise on the tensor product $L^2(\mathbb{R}) \otimes L^2(\mathbb{R}) \otimes L^2(\mathbb{R}) \cong L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$). By Steps A and B, every multi-index Hermite basis function $h_{n_1} h_{n_2} h_{n_3}$ is in the $L^2$-Cauchy completion of finite Sphere superpositions. Since the closed linear span of a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is the full space $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$, and the Cauchy completion is a closed subspace of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ containing this basis, the completion is exactly $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3 x)$. This establishes clause (i).

Clause (ii) is established by Steps A and B above: each Hermite basis function is exhibited as a Cauchy limit of finite Sphere superpositions with Gaussian source-event distributions (Step A supplying $h_0$) and polynomial weighting through the creation-operator recursion (Step B supplying $h_n$ for $n \geq 1$). $\blacksquare$

The completion is therefore exhausted by limits of countable Cauchy sequences of finite McGucken-Sphere superpositions, giving

𝓗_t := completion of (𝓥, ⟨·, ·⟩\_t) in ‖·‖\_t = L²(ℝ³, d³x),

the standard one-particle nonrelativistic Hilbert space at parameter time t.

The construction is performed at each parameter time $t \in \mathbb{R}$. The Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_t$ at parameter time $t$ is unitarily equivalent to $\mathcal{H}_{t'}$ at any other parameter time $t'$ via the McGucken-derived unitary evolution of Theorem 9.2. The unitarity descends explicitly from $\mathrm{dx}_4/\mathrm{dt} = ic$ through the following chain:

*(i) Constant-rate $x_4$-advance.* The McGucken Principle (Principle 2.1) states that $x_4$ advances at constant rate $c$ at every spacetime event — a homogeneous, conservative motion in the $x_4$-direction with no source or sink. This is the kinematic statement that the Sphere wavefront’s $x_4$-momentum is invariant along the wavefront’s worldline.

*(ii) $x_4$-flux conservation on the spatial slice.* The constant-rate $x_4$-advance implies an associated continuity equation for the McGucken-Sphere wavefront: at every spacetime point, the spatial divergence of the wavefront’s probability current is balanced by the temporal change in the probability density, $\partial_t|\psi|^2 + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{j} = 0$, where $\mathbf{j} = (\hbar/2mi)(\psi^* \nabla \psi - \psi\, \nabla \psi^*)$ is the McGucken-derived probability current (cf. §9.2.5 for the derivation of the current from Sphere-wavefront kinematics). Integrating this continuity equation over the spatial slice $\mathbb{R}^3$, with the wavefunction’s normalizable decay at spatial infinity making the boundary term vanish, gives $(d/dt) \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} |\psi|^2\, d^3x = 0$ — the $L^2$-norm $\|\psi\|^2_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)}$ is conserved under McGucken-expansion evolution (Theorem 9.2 establishes this conservation law from $x_4$-flux conservation explicitly).

*(iii) Unitary evolution from norm conservation.* The McGucken-expansion evolution preserves the geometric-overlap norm on $\mathcal{H}_t \cong L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3 x)$ by (ii). By Stone’s theorem (1930), an $L^2$-norm-preserving one-parameter evolution on a separable Hilbert space is, equivalently, a strongly-continuous one-parameter unitary group; the McGucken-derived Schrödinger generator $i\hbar\, \partial_t \psi = \hat{H} \psi$ supplied by §9.2.5 from the McGucken-Sphere wavefront’s nonrelativistic envelope dynamics is the self-adjoint generator of this unitary group.

*(iv) Parameter-time-independent identification of Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$.* The unitary map $U(t', t) : \mathcal{H}_t \to \mathcal{H}_{t'}$ generated by $\hat{H}$ establishes the unitary equivalence of $\mathcal{H}_t$ and $\mathcal{H}_{t'}$ for any pair of parameter times $t, t' \in \mathbb{R}$. The Hilbert space is therefore well-defined as

$$\mathcal{H} \cong L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3 x),$$

independent of the parameter time at which the construction is performed. The parameter-time independence is itself a $\mathrm{dx}_4/\mathrm{dt} = ic$ consequence: the constant-rate $x_4$-advance (i) forces $x_4$-flux conservation (ii), which forces $L^2$-norm conservation, which forces unitary evolution (iii), which forces parameter-time-independent identification of the Hilbert space (iv). The dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel derivation establishes Theorem 6.1.5 in the form stated above. $\blacksquare$

### 6.4.6 Convergence of dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel on the Hilbert space

The Algebraic Channel derivation of §6.4 (Stone–von Neumann uniqueness) starts from the McGucken-derived canonical commutator algebra (Theorem 5.1) and identifies the Hilbert space as the unique irreducible separable representation of the Weyl form, with the inner product determined uniquely as the invariant pairing on the irreducible representation. ### 6.6.5 The historical-foundational inversion: why the Algebraic Channel dominated history and why the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel is foundationally primary

The §6.4 (Algebraic Channel) and §6.4.5 (dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel) derivations both produce the same Hilbert space $\mathcal{H} \cong L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3x)$, with the convergence catalogued in §6.4.6 and the Sphere-role table of §6.4.7 showing that both chains rest on McGucken-Sphere geometry. By every criterion of the McGucken framework, however, **the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel is the foundationally primary route** — and by every criterion of historical record, **the Hilbert space was actually arrived at via the Algebraic Channel**. These two answers are opposite, and the disagreement is the precise signature of what the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic supplies that the prior tradition lacked. The present subsection resolves the apparent paradox via the projection-theorem reading of §16, then catalogues ten prior traditions that attempted Geometric-Channel-style derivations and identifies the specific foundational gap that prevented each of them from completing the construction.

#### 6.6.5.1 The dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel is primary

Six criteria identify the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel (§6.4.5) as the foundationally primary route:

*(1) Primitive vectors are physical, not abstract.* The dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel begins with McGucken-Sphere wavefronts $\psi_E$ as the primitive vectors of the construction (Step 1 of §6.4.5) — physical wavefronts from definite source events, each carrying the full $+ic$-oriented content of the McGucken Sphere. The Algebraic Channel begins with an abstract Hilbert space carrying a representation of the canonical commutator algebra, with the abstract space identified as $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ only through Stone-von Neumann’s uniqueness theorem in Step 6. The dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel’s primitive vectors are objects; the Algebraic Channel’s are placeholders later filled in by a uniqueness theorem.

*(2) The inner product has direct geometric meaning.* The dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel inner product $\langle \varphi, \psi \rangle = \int \varphi^* \psi\, d^3 x$ (Step 3 of §6.4.5) is the literal pointwise overlap of two Sphere wavefronts at each spatial-slice point, integrated over the slice — the geometry of “two Sphere wavefronts simultaneously present at the same spatial point”. The Algebraic Channel inner product is the abstract invariant pairing on the unique irreducible Stone-von Neumann representation, with no direct physical meaning until the representation is identified.

*(3) Each pre-Hilbert axiom traces to a specific upstream Sphere-geometric theorem.* The dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel inherits sesquilinearity from Lemma 7.1 (rank-2 metric on Sphere wavefront), conjugate symmetry from Theorem 7.11 (PT-symmetry of Sphere through source event), and positive-definiteness from Theorem 7.4 (Born density as Sphere overlap) — each axiom is supplied by an established Sphere-geometric theorem (Step 4 of §6.4.5). The Algebraic Channel inherits all three indirectly through Stone-von Neumann’s “invariant pairing” — true but downstream of an abstract representation theorem, not derived from upstream geometry.

*(4) The $+ic$ orientation is preserved.* The dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel carries the full $+ic$-oriented content of the McGucken Sphere through every step. The Algebraic Channel is sign-blind on $+ic$: the CCR $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ is preserved under the involution $T: i \to -i$ together with $\hbar \to -\hbar$ (Lemma 16.3.1), and Stone-von Neumann’s uniqueness theorem treats $+i\hbar$ and $-i\hbar$ symmetrically. By Corollary 16.4, the Algebraic Channel is the $T$-invariant projection $\Pi_A$ of the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel — the $+ic$ orientation is projected away into the sign-blind operator algebra.

*(5) Strip-the-Sphere test reveals both channels are Sphere-grounded, with different depth of grounding.* Strip the Sphere from the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel and the primitive vectors $\psi_E$ vanish — no construction at all. Strip the Sphere from the Algebraic Channel and Theorem 5.1’s derivation of the CCR collapses (no Sphere → no $x_4$-perpendicularity → no $i$ in $i\hbar$; no Sphere → no $x_4$-oscillation → no $\hbar$ in $i\hbar$) — the algebraic input also vanishes. Both routes are Sphere-grounded, but the Algebraic Channel’s Sphere-dependence is *hidden one cascade level beneath operator algebra*, whereas the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel’s Sphere-dependence is *explicit at every step*. The Algebraic Channel is the algebraic presentation of the same Sphere content; the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel is the direct geometric presentation.

*(6) Cascade-level continuity with the manifold Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$.* By Theorem 10.6 (the Hilbert-Minkowski identity), the Hilbert space and the Minkowski manifold are two presentations of the same geometric object — the constraint surface where dx₄/dt = ic holds locally. The Geometric Channel makes this continuity visible: Sphere wavefronts are functions on Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$, the Hilbert space is the function-space rendering of the same manifold, the spatial slice carries the inner product as direct integration over the manifold’s spatial slice. The Algebraic Channel obscures the continuity: the manifold disappears into the abstract Heisenberg-algebra representation, and only Stone-von Neumann’s uniqueness recovers the spatial slice as the configuration-space domain of the multiplication operator.

By every criterion, the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel is foundationally primary; the Algebraic Channel is its $T$-invariant projection $\Pi_A$.

#### 6.6.5.2 The Hilbert space historically arrived via the Algebraic Channel

The historical trajectory is exactly the reverse of the ordering. Quantum mechanics arrived at the Hilbert space *algebraically*, with the geometry suppressed at every step:

*(i) Heisenberg’s matrix mechanics (1925).* Heisenberg’s “Über quantentheoretische Umdeutung kinematischer und mechanischer Beziehungen” (*Zeitschrift für Physik* 33, 879–893) started from observable algebra and the multiplication table of position and momentum — purely algebraic, no wavefunction, no geometry. The first arrival at the operator-algebra structure that would later be recognized as the Heisenberg algebra $\mathfrak{h}_3$.

*(ii) Born–Jordan formalization (1925).* “Zur Quantenmechanik” (*ZP* 34, 858–888) derived the canonical commutation relation $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ explicitly as the algebra of Heisenberg’s multiplication table. Algebraic.

*(iii) Born–Heisenberg–Jordan, the* Drei-Männer-Arbeit *(1926).* “Zur Quantenmechanik II” (*ZP* 35, 557–615) extended matrix mechanics to a complete algebraic framework. Algebraic.

*(iv) Schrödinger’s wave mechanics (1926, four papers).* The only historically Geometric-Channel-like development: Schrödinger derived the wave equation from de Broglie’s wave-particle duality, with $\psi$ as a wavefunction satisfying a PDE on spacetime (“Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem”, I–IV, *Annalen der Physik* 79–81). Critically, however, *Schrödinger had no foundational geometric principle* from which to derive $\psi$. He guessed at the wave equation by promoting the classical Hamilton-Jacobi equation through Hamilton’s 1828 optical-mechanical analogy. The wavefunction $\psi$ was an *input* to the theory, but without a dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel *foundation*. Schrödinger himself misinterpreted $\psi$ as a physical charge density spread over space (the “matter wave” reading), which was empirically wrong.

*(v) Born’s probabilistic interpretation (1926).* “Zur Quantenmechanik der Stoßvorgänge” (*ZP* 37, 863–867). Born proposed $|\psi|^2$ as the probability density of finding the particle at a position. This single move **demoted $\psi$ from a physical wave to a probability amplitude** — projecting away precisely the geometry that Schrödinger’s wave mechanics carried. After Born, $\psi$ was no longer a wavefront on spacetime; it was a calculational device for computing probabilities, and the only fact about it that mattered was the abstract structure $|\psi|^2\, d^3x$ as a probability measure.

*(vi) Schrödinger’s equivalence proof (1926).* “Über das Verhältnis der Heisenberg-Born-Jordanschen Quantenmechanik zu der meinen” (*AdP* 79, 734–756). Schrödinger proved that wave mechanics and matrix mechanics give the same predictions. Crucially, this proof was unidirectional in influence: it cemented matrix mechanics as the “real” theory and wave mechanics as “one representation of it”, rather than the reverse.

*(vii) Dirac’s transformation theory (1925–1930).* Culminating in *Principles of Quantum Mechanics* (Oxford, 1930), Dirac built the abstract framework of state vectors and operators on an abstract Hilbert space. The wavefunction became one possible representation of an abstract state vector. Algebraic and representational throughout.

*(viii) Stone’s theorem and von Neumann’s uniqueness (1930–31).* Stone, “Linear transformations in Hilbert space III” (*Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci.* 16, 172–175); von Neumann, “Die Eindeutigkeit der Schrödingerschen Operatoren” (*Mathematische Annalen* 104, 570–578). The Weyl form of the CCR has a unique irreducible separable representation up to unitary equivalence — namely $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ with the Schrödinger representation. **This is the moment the Algebraic Channel completed.** From the Heisenberg algebra alone, the Hilbert space was forced to be $L^2$ — no geometric input required, no wave-mechanical reading needed.

*(ix) Von Neumann’s axiomatic codification (1932).* *Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik* (Springer). Axiomatic formalization of QM in Hilbert space language. The Hilbert space became *the* foundational object of quantum mechanics. The wavefunction $\psi$ was deemphasized as an element of an abstract Hilbert space; the operator algebra became central. **This was the canonical Algebraic Channel arrival.**

*(x) Feynman’s path integral (1948).* “Space-time approach to non-relativistic quantum mechanics” (*Rev. Mod. Phys.* 20, 367–387). Reconstructed QM from path-summation amplitudes $\psi = \sum_\gamma \exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$. This is the *closest historical predecessor to the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel* — $\psi$ as a path-integral kernel on spacetime, with phase from action, with Huygens-like superposition over paths. Feynman supplied no upstream geometric principle for the action $S$ or the phase $\exp(iS/\hbar)$; the path-integral formulation was equivalent to the canonical formulation (Dyson’s later equivalence proof), not foundational to it.

The historical pattern shows consistent **algebraic dominance with geometric demotion**: at every juncture where a Geometric-Channel-like reading was available, it was demoted in favor of an Algebraic-Channel reading. Schrödinger’s wave mechanics was demoted to a representation of matrix mechanics; Schrödinger’s physical-wave reading of $\psi$ was demoted to Born’s probability amplitude; von Neumann’s axiomatization enshrined Hilbert space as primitive with $\psi$ as element; Feynman’s path integral was presented as equivalent reformulation, not foundational.

The reason is twofold. **First, historical contingency**: Heisenberg published first by a few months, the Copenhagen interpretation emphasized measurement and operator algebra over wave, and von Neumann’s 1932 axiomatization solidified the Algebraic Channel as the foundational framework before wave-mechanical content could be developed into a geometric foundation. **Second, inaccessibility**: the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel requires an upstream principle from which Sphere wavefronts can be derived. Without such a principle, $\psi$ has to be guessed at (Schrödinger) or postulated (Feynman path integral). The Algebraic Channel could proceed without any geometric grounding — just algebra, representations, and Stone-von Neumann uniqueness — so it was the path of least resistance for a century.

#### 6.6.5.3 The McGucken inversion via the projection theorem (cross-reference to §16)

The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework supplies what was missing for a hundred years: a foundational principle (dx₄/dt = ic) from which the Sphere wavefront is a theorem (not an input), the Hilbert space is a theorem (Theorems 6.1 and 6.1.5), the Born rule is a theorem (Theorem 7.2), the CCR is a theorem (Theorem 5.1), and the Schrödinger equation is a theorem (Theorems 9.0.5 and 9.1). This converts the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel from a side-stream of historical wave mechanics — wave without foundation — into the foundational route, with the Algebraic Channel recovered as its $T$-invariant projection $\Pi_A$ (the algebraic shadow that history privileged because the foundational principle was missing).

The projection-theorem reading of §16 supplies the precise resolution of the apparent paradox:

*Foundational ordering*: dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel is primary because it carries the full $+ic$-oriented content of the McGucken Sphere; Algebraic Channel is the $T$-invariant projection $\Pi_A$ of the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel (Lemma 16.3.1, Corollary 16.4), with $+ic$ orientation projected away.

*Historical ordering*: The Algebraic Channel (the projection $\Pi_A$) was accessible without the foundational principle dx₄/dt = ic, because the algebra of operators carries enough structure (Stone-von Neumann uniqueness) to fix the representation. The dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel (the unprojected source) requires dx₄/dt = ic to derive Sphere wavefronts as theorems. Without dx₄/dt = ic, history could only access the projection.

*The orthodox foundational confusion* (§16.17) is the canonical case of treating the algebraic shadow as the source: ninety-four years of foundational reconstructions all operated within the Algebraic Channel, treating Hilbert space as ontologically primitive when it is in fact the function-space rendering of the McGucken-derived Minkowski manifold (Theorem 10.6) — the algebraic shadow $\Pi_A$ of the Sphere’s geometry, mistaken for the source for a century.

So: the natural answer (Geometric is more natural and fuller) and the historical answer (Algebraic was the route taken) are *both* correct, and their disagreement is the precise signature of what dx₄/dt = ic provides that the prior tradition lacked. History followed the projection because the source was inaccessible without the foundational principle. With dx₄/dt = ic in place, the source becomes derivable and the historical ordering reverses.

#### 6.6.5.4 Prior attempts at Geometric-Channel-style derivations: a ten-tradition survey

Various programs in the prior literature attempted derivations of QM’s Hilbert space that carried geometry beyond the pure Algebraic Channel. The present subsection catalogues these prior attempts, identifies the closest match to the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel in each case, and pinpoints the specific foundational gap that prevented each program from completing the construction. **No prior program derived the Hilbert space from a single foundational geometric-kinematic principle in the way the McGucken framework does from dx₄/dt = ic**; the ten traditions captured various *fragments* of the geometry but always either as input (postulated) or as output of a theory that itself assumed Hilbert-space structure.

*(A) Wave-mechanical tradition.* Hamilton (1828) — “On a general method in dynamics”, *Phil. Trans. Roy. Soc.* — established the optical-mechanical analogy: surfaces of constant action propagate like wavefronts. De Broglie (1924) — *Recherches sur la théorie des Quanta* (PhD thesis); “Ondes et quanta”, *Comptes Rendus* 177, 507–510 — postulated matter waves $\lambda = h/p$. Schrödinger (1926) — four “Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem” papers in *Annalen der Physik* 79–81 — derived the wave equation by promoting the Hamilton-Jacobi equation through Hamilton’s analogy and matching with hydrogen spectra. Bohm (1952) — “A suggested interpretation of the quantum theory in terms of ‘hidden’ variables”, *Phys. Rev.* 85, 166–193 — pilot-wave theory with $\psi$ as a real physical guidance field. Bohm-Hiley (1993) — *The Undivided Universe* (Routledge) — extended pilot-wave to the quantum-potential reading. *Closest match to dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel*: $\psi$ as a wavefunction on spacetime carrying geometry. *Gap*: no foundational principle generating $\psi$; in each case the wavefunction is postulated, not derived. Schrödinger’s $\psi$ was guessed at via Hamilton’s optical-mechanical analogy; de Broglie’s matter wave was postulated; Bohm’s pilot wave was an interpretive overlay on the already-postulated Schrödinger $\psi$.

*The expanding light sphere as the common derivational root of both relativity and wave mechanics.* A historical fact worth stating exactly: the founders of both relativity and wave mechanics reached their theories through the expanding spherical wavefront, and did so independently. Einstein (1905), in §3 of “Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper,” emitted a spherical light wave $x^2+y^2+z^2 = c^2t^2$ and required that under the Lorentz transformation it remain a spherical wave expanding at $c$, $\xi^2+\eta^2+\zeta^2 = c^2\tau^2$ — the form-invariance of the light sphere is his derivation of the Lorentz transformation (Pierseaux 2004, *physics/0411045*, which contrasts Einstein’s spherical wavefront with Poincaré’s rival ellipsoidal one; and Walter 2018, cited in §2.4.4). Einstein used the sphere again in 1911, now in its Huygens form: to derive the bending of light in a gravitational field he drew the secondary wavelets emitted from points on a wavefront and took their envelope as the next wavefront, the wavefront bending because the wavelets on the deeper-potential side travel slower — an explicit Huygens secondary-wavelet construction, with Einstein’s own historic figure, outlining general relativity. Schrödinger (1926), in his second and more physical derivation, built wave mechanics on the same wavefront geometry: combining the principles of Hamilton, Huygens, and Fermat through the optical-mechanical analogy, he propagated surfaces of constant action as Huygens wavefronts and matched the resulting eigenvalue problem to the hydrogen spectrum. The two foundational theories of twentieth-century physics were therefore both derived from the expanding spherical wavefront and its Huygens propagation — Einstein’s light sphere for relativity, Schrödinger’s Huygens surfaces of action for wave mechanics. The two uses are individually documented; what the present framework adds is their unification: the expanding sphere both men used is one physical object, the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p)$, the wavefront of the $x_4$-expansion $dx_4/dt = ic$. Relativity is the covariance of that sphere (§2.4.4) and wave mechanics is the same sphere carrying an action quantum $\hbar$ per Huygens cycle (§2.3, §4.3). Einstein and Schrödinger reached the two theories through the same geometric object without a principle identifying it as one physical thing; $dx_4/dt = ic$ supplies that principle, so the shared wavefront becomes the common derivational root rather than a historical coincidence of method.

*The Kirchhoff quarter-wave factor as the i of dx₄/dt = ic.* The identification of the shared wavefront as the McGucken Sphere permits a derivation that the standard optics literature leaves as an inserted convention: the origin of the mandatory factor $1/(i\lambda) = -i/\lambda$ that multiplies every secondary wavelet in the Fresnel–Kirchhoff diffraction integral. In the standard treatment this quarter-wave prefactor — a $90^\circ$ phase advance, $e^{-i\pi/2}$, of each secondary wavelet relative to the primary wave — is fixed by requiring that the Huygens construction reproduce the forward-propagating wave; Fresnel inserted it by hand and Kirchhoff justified it from the Green’s-function structure of the wave equation, in each case as a property of the scalar diffraction integral rather than of an underlying physical process. Under dx₄/dt = ic the prefactor is forced, and the imaginary unit it carries is the same i as in the Principle.

The derivation proceeds in five steps, each resting on a result already established in the corpus. First, the secondary wavelet is propagated by the McGucken Operator flow $\Phi^s = e^{s D_M}$, $D_M = \partial_t + ic\,\partial_{x_4}$, which advances the wavefront by $ic\,s$ along $x_4$; the generator of the advance carries the factor $ic$, so the i is the coefficient of the wavelet’s advance, not an external label (Reciprocal Generation, Corollary 19 \[MG-Reciprocal\]; and §5.2 for the i as the perpendicularity marker of x₄). Second, a single secondary wavelet is the outgoing spherical kernel $e^{ikr}/r$, the elementary Huygens source of the propagator read as the x₄-coherent Huygens kernel (\[MG-PathInt\]; \[MG-Feynman\], Proposition III.1). Third, the next wavefront is the superposition of these wavelets over the surface of the expanding McGucken Sphere, $U(P) = C \int\!\int U(Q)\,(e^{ikr}/r)\,K(\chi)\,dS$ — the Huygens forward-envelope construction (\[MG-Feynman\], Proposition II.5; Reciprocal Generation, Theorem 51 \[MG-Reciprocal\]). Fourth, the superposition itself manufactures a factor of $+i$: evaluating it by stationary phase, the transverse spreading of the wavelets over the two dimensions of the wavefront gives, for each transverse direction, a Fresnel factor $e^{i\pi/4}$, and the two together give $e^{i\pi/4}\cdot e^{i\pi/4} = e^{i\pi/2} = +i$. The $+i$ is the signature of the *sphericity* of the McGucken Sphere: the wavefront is a 2-sphere, expanding in the two directions transverse to the propagation, and each transverse direction contributes $45^\circ$, summing to the $90^\circ$ that the imaginary unit marks. Fifth, consistency of the Huygens construction — the requirement that the envelope reproduce the forward wave — forces the prefactor to cancel this $+i$: $C = 1/(i\lambda) = -i/\lambda$. The Kirchhoff quarter-wave factor is therefore the reciprocal of the $+i$ produced by the two-dimensional spherical spreading of the McGucken Sphere’s secondary wavelets.

The i cancelled is the same i as in dx₄/dt = ic. It arose in step four from the spreading of wavelets whose advance is generated by the ic in $D_M$ (steps one and two), and it is a $90^\circ$ rotation produced by the two spreading directions being perpendicular to the propagation direction — the same perpendicularity that the i marks in x₄ = ict, where the fourth coordinate is perpendicular to the three spatial dimensions (§5.2). The two transverse directions each contribute $45^\circ$ exactly because the expansion is spherically symmetric, so the $90^\circ$ is the geometric record of the sphere’s two-dimensional transverse curvature. The quarter-wave factor that Fresnel inserted by hand is thus the fingerprint of the expanding fourth dimension: the same imaginary unit, the same perpendicularity, now read as the phase advance of an expanding spherical wavefront. Removing the i — the real (++++) reading of the fourth axis — removes the spherical spreading’s $90^\circ$ advance and with it the Kirchhoff prefactor, which is why a real proper-time coordinate reproduces geometric optics but not the phase structure of wave propagation.

*Scope.* What is derived is that the $-i$ prefactor is the reciprocal of the $+i$ generated by two-dimensional spherical (Fresnel) spreading, and that this $+i$ traces to the ic-generated advance of the wavelets — a computation, verifiable by the stationary-phase evaluation of the Fresnel integral (each transverse quadrature contributing $e^{i\pi/4}$). The identification of this i with the x₄-perpendicularity i of the Principle rests on both being $90^\circ$ rotations arising from perpendicular directions — the two transverse spreading directions here, x₄ against the spatial three in the metric — the same perpendicularity reading that grounds the shared-i result of §5.2 and Bohr’s 1937 observation (ref. \[210\]).

Feynman (1948) — “Space-time approach to non-relativistic quantum mechanics”, *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 20, 367–387 — reconstructed QM from path-integral kernels $\psi = \sum_\gamma \exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$. The path-integral formulation was equivalent to canonical quantization (Dyson’s later equivalence proof), not foundational to it. ### 6.6.6 The null-structure prerequisite: why Cauchy completeness presupposes the McGucken Sphere, and how the null structure enters every derivation of the physical QM Hilbert space

§6.6.5 catalogued ten distinct prior traditions that attempted geometric or geometric-adjacent derivations of QM’s Hilbert space, identifying the specific foundational gap that prevented each from completing the construction without the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic. The present subsection sharpens that analysis by isolating one specific prerequisite — the Lorentzian null structure — and tracing its appearance across all ten traditions. The conclusion is that **no derivation of the physical QM Hilbert space avoids the null structure**; what differs across derivations is the depth at which it enters and whether it is foundational input or downstream coupling. The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel is distinguished from all ten prior traditions by having the null structure as the foundational input — the McGucken Sphere $\mathcal{M}_E(t)$ is the null surface, generated directly from dx₄/dt = ic via Lemma 2.5 — rather than as a downstream feature added when the abstract Hilbert space is coupled to spacetime.

#### 6.6.6.1 Disambiguating “null vectors”

The term “null vector” has two distinct meanings that must be separated before the analysis begins:

*(i) Linear-algebra sense*: the zero vector $\mathbf{0}$, the identity element of vector addition. Every vector space, including every Hilbert space, must contain $\mathbf{0}$ by axiom. A Hilbert space without $\mathbf{0}$ is impossible by definition. This is the trivial reading and not the subject of the present subsection.

*(ii) Lorentzian sense*: non-zero vectors $v$ in a Lorentzian inner-product space satisfying $\langle v, v \rangle = 0$ — that is, vectors on the light cone. The McGucken Sphere $\mathcal{M}_E(t) = \{p : ds^2(E, p) = 0,\, x_4(p) - x_4(E) = ict\}$ (Definition 2.3) **is** the null surface — the locus of points at null separation from the source event $E$ at parameter time $t$. The Sphere is the null cone intersected with the constant-$x_4$ hypersurface; the null cone is the Sphere.

In what follows “null vectors” means the Lorentzian-sense reading throughout, since this is the interesting case. The question is: *can the physical QM Hilbert space be Cauchy complete without the Lorentzian null structure?*

#### 6.6.6.2 The McGucken QM Hilbert space cannot exist without null vectors: a six-step construction-prerequisite walkthrough

In the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel derivation of §6.4.5, every step of the Hilbert-space construction depends on the null structure being present. The dependence is derivational at each step.

*Step 1 — Primitive vectors.* The primitive vectors of the construction are Sphere wavefronts $\psi_E$ (Step 1 of §6.4.5). The Sphere is the null surface $\{p : ds^2(E, p) = 0\}$ (Definition 2.3). Strip the null vectors and there is no Sphere; strip the Sphere and there are no primitive vectors. The construction has nothing to start from.

*Step 2 — Linear combinations.* Finite linear combinations $\sum_E c_E \psi_E$ are the pre-Hilbert vectors (Step 2 of §6.4.5). Each summand is a Sphere wavefront riding the null cone of $E$; the superposition is a sum of null-cone contributions weighted by amplitudes. Without null vectors there are no Sphere wavefronts to superpose, and the linearity-from-universality argument of Theorem 2.4 (iv) has nothing to apply to.

*Step 3 — Inner product.* The inner product $\langle \varphi, \psi \rangle = \int \varphi^* \psi\, d^3 x$ (Step 3 of §6.4.5) is the pointwise overlap of two Sphere wavefronts at each spatial-slice point, integrated over the slice. The “overlap” is the simultaneous presence of two null-cone wavefronts at the same spatial point. Theorem 7.4 derives the Born density $|\psi(x)|^2$ as the overlap of two Sphere wavefronts at $x$ — and this overlap is a null-structure statement: the integrand at point $x$ is the contribution to the wavefronts of source events whose null cones pass through $x$ at parameter time $t$.

*Step 4 — Pre-Hilbert axioms.* Each of the three pre-Hilbert axioms traces to a Sphere-geometric theorem that depends on the null structure (Step 4 of §6.4.5):

-   *Sesquilinearity* from Lemma 7.1 (rank-2 metric on Sphere wavefront). The rank-2 character is a direct consequence of the Lorentzian signature, which exists precisely because of the null structure $(ict)^2 = -c^2 t^2$ (Lemma 2.5).

-   *Conjugate symmetry* from Theorem 7.11 (PT-symmetry of Sphere through source event). The Sphere’s PT-symmetry is the symmetry of the null cone under simultaneous spatial inversion and time reversal through $E$. No null structure → no Sphere → no PT-symmetry → no conjugate symmetry of the inner product.

-   *Positive-definiteness* from Theorem 7.4 (Born density as Sphere overlap). The integrand $|\psi(x)|^2$ is positive because it is a real non-negative function of the Sphere wavefront’s null-cone amplitude at $x$. Strip the Sphere and there is nothing to integrate.

*Step 5 — Density and the Hermite lemma* (Lemma 6.1.6). This is where the question of Cauchy completeness becomes sharpest. Lemma 6.1.6 establishes density via the Hermite functions, derived from Gaussian source-event distributions on the McGucken Sphere. Every input to this density argument depends on the null structure:

-   Gaussian source distributions $\rho_\sigma(p) = \exp(-|p - p_0|^2 / 2\sigma^2)$ have no surface to live on without the Sphere.
-   The free-evolution operator $U_\text{free}(t)$ (Theorem 9.0.5) requires the Sphere mass-shell and Compton frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ — both depend on the Lorentzian structure.
-   The position operator $\hat{x}$ has no translation-invariant Sphere assignment to translate (Theorem 2.4 (iv) universality clause).
-   The momentum operator $\hat{p}$ has no spatial slice — no Lorentzian metric → no spacelike hypersurface → no constant-$x_4$ slice.
-   The Hermite functions $h_n$ have nothing to be a basis *of*.

*Step 6 — Cauchy completion.* Take the metric completion of finite Sphere-wavefront combinations under the norm $\|\psi\| = \sqrt{\langle \psi, \psi \rangle}$. This is the construction that produces $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3 x)$. But Cauchy completion requires a space to complete. The completion is *of* finite linear combinations of Sphere wavefronts. Without null vectors there are no Sphere wavefronts, hence no space to complete, hence no Cauchy completion. **The completion is not optional; it presupposes the null structure as its raw material.** The completion does not manufacture the null structure; the null structure must already be present in the pre-Hilbert space being completed.

#### 6.6.6.3 The four-fold ontology: photons ARE the null vectors of the dx₄/dt = ic framework

The four-fold ontology of the McGucken framework (Principle 2.1) makes the null-vector prerequisite concrete:

(1) Massive particle at spatial rest: full $c$-budget into $x_4$ — dx₄/dt = ic, *timelike* worldline.

(2) Photon: Sphere-tangent share $v_{x_4} = 0$ (Principle dx₄/dt = ic holding), absolute rest in $x_4$ — *null* worldline.

(3) Absolute motion = $x_4$-expansion at $ic$ — *timelike* directionality.

(4) CMB frame = isotropic cosmological $x_4$-expansion — *timelike* foliation.

The photon ontology (case 2) is the null-worldline case. **Photons literally** ***are*** **the null vectors of the dx₄/dt = ic framework.** They ride the McGucken Sphere as wavefronts at null. Strip the null structure and one does not just lose a corner of the ontology; one loses the entire relationship between massive particles and photons, between rest-frame $x_4$-oscillation and spatial wavefront propagation, between the Compton frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ and the photon frequency $\omega = ck$ at the relativistic limit. The Lorentzian structure $(ict)^2 = -c^2 t^2$ that generates the null cone is exactly what makes the rest-mass-to-photon-frequency coupling work, and this coupling is what makes the wavefunction $\psi$ a physical object on spacetime rather than an abstract algebraic placeholder. The null structure is therefore not a feature one could remove from the dx₄/dt = ic framework while keeping the rest intact; it is constitutive of the dx₄/dt = ic framework’s content.

#### 6.6.6.4 Abstract Cauchy completeness versus physical Cauchy completeness

The question “can the Hilbert space be Cauchy complete without null vectors?” admits two cleanly separable cases.

*As pure mathematics — yes.* Abstract Hilbert spaces exist without any null-vector structure. The classical examples — $\ell^2(\mathbb{C})$ of square-summable complex sequences, $L^2[0,1]$ of square-integrable functions on the unit interval, $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n, d\mu)$ for any positive measure $\mu$ — are Cauchy complete inner-product spaces with no reference to any Lorentzian metric, no light cone, no $ds^2 = 0$ surface. Cauchy completeness is a topological property of the metric induced by the inner product; it makes no demand on the underlying geometry of any spacetime, because in pure mathematics there is no spacetime. The Cauchy completeness of $\ell^2(\mathbb{C})$ is a theorem of real analysis — every Cauchy sequence in $\ell^2$ has a limit in $\ell^2$ — independent of any physical interpretation.

*As the physical QM Hilbert space derived from dx₄/dt = ic — no.* The specific Hilbert space of quantum mechanics is $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3 x)$ with the position eigenstate basis, the canonical commutator, the Schrödinger evolution, the Born rule, and the rest of the physical apparatus. By Theorem 10.6 (the Hilbert-Minkowski identity), this $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3, d^3 x)$ is the function-space rendering of the constraint surface where dx₄/dt = ic holds locally — equivalently, it is $L^2(\mathbb{M}_{1,3})$, the Minkowski manifold in its function-valued representation. The Lorentzian structure of Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ — the null cone at every event, the Sphere $\mathcal{M}_E(t)$ as the locus of null separation from $E$ — is part of the geometric data that the Hilbert space is the function-space rendering of. Strip the null vectors and one does not get a different Hilbert space; one gets no Hilbert space at all in this construction, because there is nothing for the function-space rendering to render.

This bifurcation between abstract and physical Cauchy completeness is the key to understanding how prior derivations of QM’s Hilbert space relate to the null structure: prior derivations land on the *abstract* side of the bifurcation, deriving a Cauchy-complete Hilbert space that becomes physical only after spacetime coupling. The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel lands on the *physical* side directly, deriving the physical Hilbert space from the foundational kinematic principle without an intermediate abstract step.

#### 6.6.6.5 The null-structure prerequisite across the ten derivational traditions

The pattern is this: **the null vectors are present as they are part of what makes a Hilbert space the physical QM Hilbert space.** Stripping the null structure leaves one with an abstract Cauchy-complete inner-product space that is isomorphic to $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ as a vector space, but is no longer the QM Hilbert space, because all the structure that makes it QM — the position observable, the momentum observable, the canonical commutator, the Hamiltonian, the Born rule, the unitary dynamics — depends on the Lorentzian-spacetime geometry that the null vectors are part of.

The remainder of the present subsection traces this pattern through the ten traditions catalogued in §6.6.5.4. For each tradition, the analysis identifies (α) what the derivation produces (abstract or physical Hilbert space), (β) whether null structure is explicit in the construction, and (γ) where the null structure enters if not explicit (typically: spacetime coupling, relativistic embedding, or $c \to \infty$ contraction).

*(A) Wave-mechanical tradition (Schrödinger 1926, de Broglie 1924, Bohm 1952).* Schrödinger derived the wave equation by promoting the Hamilton-Jacobi equation via Hamilton’s optical-mechanical analogy. The wavefunction $\psi(x,t)$ lives on configuration space × time. Cauchy completion of wavepackets to $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is the analytical step. Null structure appears *explicitly* when the theory is made relativistic (Klein-Gordon, Dirac), where the mass shell $p^2 = m^2 c^2$ and the light cone $p^2 = 0$ are explicit. In the nonrelativistic limit Schrödinger started with, the null structure is *hidden in the dispersion relation* $E = p^2/2m + V$, which is the $c \to \infty$ limit of the relativistic dispersion $E^2 = p^2 c^2 + m^2 c^4$. The light cones open out to flat horizontal hyperplanes — the null structure becomes degenerate and one obtains Galilean spacetime with its degenerate “null cones” at infinity. The Hilbert space one gets is the same $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$, but the foundational geometry has changed from Lorentzian to Galilean. The nonrelativistic Hilbert space *could* be Cauchy-complete without explicit null vectors — but only in the artificial $c \to \infty$ limit. The moment one asks why $\hbar$ has the value it does, why the dispersion relation has the form it does, why the wavefunction is complex, why electrons have spin, why the Pauli equation embeds in the Dirac equation, why scattering amplitudes obey causality — every one of these takes one back to the Lorentzian structure with null cones. The nonrelativistic Hilbert space is a low-energy approximation; the Lorentzian structure is the full story, and it is there even in nonrelativistic QM, just suppressed. Bohm’s pilot wave (1952) and Bohm-Hiley (1993) inherit this dependence completely.

*(B) Path-integral tradition (Dirac 1933, Feynman 1948).* Feynman’s path integral $\psi(x, t) = \int \mathcal{D}\gamma\, \exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)\, \psi(x_0, t_0)$ sums over paths in configuration space. Nonrelativistically, the action $S = \int (T - V)\, dt$ has no explicit null structure. But the relativistic path integral sums over timelike or null worldlines, with the propagator vanishing outside the light cone. The nonrelativistic propagator is the $c \to \infty$ contraction of this. The famous “propagation faster than light” of the nonrelativistic Schrödinger propagator — the kernel $K(x, t; x_0, 0) = (m/2\pi i\hbar t)^{3/2} \exp(im(x-x_0)^2/2\hbar t)$ has support outside any finite cone — is the price of taking that limit. The Hilbert space inherited is the same $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$, but its claim to physical correctness rests on its being the limit of a relativistically-causal theory whose propagators *do* respect the light cone. Feynman-Hibbs (1965) treat the relativistic propagator with the $i\epsilon$ prescription that selects forward-light-cone propagation — the null structure is right there in the $i\epsilon$ contour, compressed into a regularization rule.

*(C) Geometric quantization (Souriau 1966, Kostant 1970).* Geometric quantization takes a symplectic manifold $(M, \omega)$ as input and produces a Hilbert space as the $L^2$ completion of polarized sections of a prequantum line bundle. The symplectic manifold has no built-in null structure; it is a $2n$-dimensional manifold with a closed non-degenerate 2-form. Does the resulting Hilbert space have null structure? **Not until coupled to spacetime.** Geometric quantization of $T^*\mathbb{R}^3 = \mathbb{R}^6$ (the phase space of a free particle) gives $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ — Cauchy-complete, infinite-dimensional, separable, with position eigenstates and the canonical commutator. No light cone anywhere in the construction. But this $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is *not yet* the physical QM Hilbert space. It is an abstract Hilbert space that *can be* coupled to a Hamiltonian. The moment one puts in a Hamiltonian — say $\hat{H} = \hat{p}^2/2m$ — one is making a choice that connects this $L^2$ to Galilean spacetime, where the dynamics happens. Once one asks about relativistic invariance via the Wigner classification of irreducible Poincaré representations, null vectors (massless representations) and timelike vectors (massive representations) enter explicitly; the Galilean limit is the contracted version. So geometric quantization derives an abstract $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ that *becomes* the physical QM Hilbert space only after spacetime coupling, and that coupling brings in the null structure either openly (relativistic case) or by suppression (Galilean limit).

*(D) Twistor theory (Penrose 1967).* Twistor theory builds spacetime out of null geodesics — twistor space $\mathbb{CP}^3$ encodes Minkowski space as the space of (complexified) null lines. The light cone is the *foundational input*: a twistor $Z^\alpha$ is essentially a null line in Minkowski space, and the twistor formalism’s primary objects (massless fields, scattering amplitudes) live naturally on null geodesics. The (pre-)Hilbert space of twistor theory (Tsuda 2012, *J. Math. Phys.*, arXiv:1210.0349) is constructed from twistor functions / cohomology classes, with the inner product defined via Penrose’s contour-integral formula or via the cohomological Eastwood construction. **Null structure is maximally explicit** — there is literally no twistor theory without null lines. Cauchy completeness of the twistor Hilbert space is a non-trivial open problem precisely because twistor theory takes the null structure seriously enough that the completion is delicate. Twistor theory shows the opposite of what one might naively expect: when null structure is taken as *fundamental* rather than derived, the Hilbert-space construction becomes harder, not easier, because more geometry is being carried. This is in deep agreement with the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel, where the price of foundational rigor is a more demanding (but more rigorous) Hilbert-space construction.

*(E) Geometric algebra and Clifford algebra (Hestenes 1966).* Hestenes’ spacetime algebra $\mathcal{C}\!\ell_{1,3}$ is the Clifford algebra of Minkowski space — built from the basis vectors $\gamma_0, \gamma_1, \gamma_2, \gamma_3$ satisfying $\gamma_\mu \gamma_\nu + \gamma_\nu \gamma_\mu = 2\eta_{\mu\nu}$, where $\eta$ is the Minkowski metric with signature $(+,-,-,-)$. **The null cone is built into the metric $\eta$, hence built into the Clifford algebra at the level of the generating relations.** Hestenes’ reformulation of the Dirac equation in spacetime algebra (Hestenes 1973, *J. Math. Phys.* 14, 893–905) makes the null structure absolutely explicit: spinors $\psi$ are even elements of $\mathcal{C}\!\ell_{1,3}$, the imaginary unit $i$ of QM is identified with a specific bivector (a spatial plane perpendicular to the spin axis), and the Dirac equation $\gamma^\mu \partial_\mu \psi = m \psi\, i\sigma_3$ has the null structure encoded in the $\gamma^\mu$ contraction. The Hilbert space inherited from Hestenes’ approach is the standard QM Hilbert space; null vectors are present at the level of the foundational algebra. Hestenes’ approach cannot Cauchy-complete a non-null version of the construction because the Clifford algebra itself fails to exist without the Lorentzian signature.

*(F) Stochastic mechanics (Nelson 1966).* Nelson derives the Schrödinger equation from a stochastic process (Brownian motion) on configuration space. The Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is the receiving structure for the probability densities. In nonrelativistic Nelson, no explicit null structure. The Brownian process lives on Galilean spacetime. The Hilbert space is Cauchy complete via standard $L^2$ analysis. But relativistic stochastic mechanics (Guerra–Marra, Loffredo, Kuipers 2021 arXiv:2102.00392, and Stueckelberg–Schrödinger approaches) requires the stochastic process to be defined on Lorentzian spacetime, and the null structure enters explicitly through the diffusion tensor. As with the wave-mechanical and path-integral cases, the nonrelativistic version suppresses the null structure into a $c \to \infty$ limit; the relativistic version restores it.

*(G) Geometrodynamics (Wheeler 1957).* Wheeler’s geometrodynamic program took GR’s spacetime — Lorentzian, with null cones at every event — as the foundational object. “Everything is geometry” meant *Lorentzian* geometry. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation for quantum cosmology applies QM to the geometry itself, with the Hilbert space being a wavefunctional space on the configuration space of 3-metrics. **Null structure is explicit at the GR level**; the Wheeler–DeWitt Hilbert space is built on top. Misner–Thorne–Wheeler (1973) is uncompromising about the Lorentzian character. Wheeler’s “It from Bit” (1989) was an attempt to derive even the Lorentzian structure from informational primitives, but Wheeler never completed this — the null structure remained input.

*(H) Noncommutative geometry (Connes 1985).* The spectral triple $(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{H}, D)$ takes the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ as **input**. So strictly speaking, Connes’ framework does not derive the Hilbert space at all — it characterizes geometries by which Hilbert spaces and Dirac operators they admit. For the standard physical case (Minkowski or Riemannian manifold), the Dirac operator $D$ encodes the Lorentzian (or Euclidean, in the Wick-rotated case) metric, including the null structure. Connes’ reconstruction of the Standard Model uses a *Euclidean* spectral triple — no null structure in the strict sense — but the Wick rotation back to Lorentzian is implicit, and the Standard Model itself has null structure at the Minkowski level. So Connes’ framework is indifferent to whether Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ has null content; it accepts whatever Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ is supplied. The physical Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ of QM has null structure (via Theorem 10.6 of the present paper, via spacetime coupling); the *abstract* Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ of a spectral triple need not.

*(I) Loop quantum gravity (Ashtekar 1986, Rovelli–Smolin 1990).* LQG uses Ashtekar variables — SU(2) connections on a spatial 3-manifold. The kinematical Hilbert space of LQG is built from spin networks; it is Cauchy complete in the natural inner product on cylindrical functions. No explicit null structure in the kinematical Hilbert space itself. But LQG is intended as a theory of quantum gravity, so the *output* is supposed to recover Lorentzian spacetime with its null cones in the semiclassical limit. The Lorentzian structure is the target, even though it does not appear in the kinematical Hilbert space. The relation between LQG’s Hilbert space and the standard $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$ of nonrelativistic QM remains an open problem; matter coupling and the continuum limit are where the null structure would enter.

*(J) Operational/informational reconstructions (Hardy 2001, CDP 2011, MGM 2019, etc.).* **This is the most interesting case for the present question, because this is where the null structure can be most cleanly suppressed.** Hardy’s “Quantum theory from five reasonable axioms” (2001) derives an abstract Hilbert-space structure from operational axioms about measurements, probabilities, and composition. Chiribella–D’Ariano–Perinotti (2011) derives it from six informational axioms. Masanes–Galley–Müller (2019) shows the measurement postulates are operationally redundant. None of these reconstructions has any mention of light cones, null vectors, or Lorentzian metrics. The abstract Hilbert space they derive — call it $\mathcal{H}_\text{op}$ — is Cauchy complete by axiom. It has continuous-spectrum observables, complex inner product, unitary evolution, the works. **It contains no null vectors and presupposes no null structure.** So: can the Hilbert space be Cauchy complete without null vectors via operational reconstruction? **Yes, abstractly.** But here is the catch. The operational reconstructions derive a Hilbert space *with no specified observable algebra*. To make it physical — to get position eigenstates with continuous spectrum, canonical commutator $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$, Schrödinger Hamiltonian $\hat{H} = \hat{p}^2/2m + V$ — one has to choose a representation, which means coupling to spacetime. The moment one does, one is back to the wave-mechanical / path-integral / Galilean-spacetime situation, with the null structure either explicit (relativistic) or suppressed (nonrelativistic). Hardy and CDP recognize this. Hardy’s later papers on operator tensors, duotensors, and operational frameworks for quantum gravity (2007, 2011, 2016) explicitly try to extend the reconstruction to relativistic spacetime, where null structure has to enter. The operational reconstructions do not *forbid* null structure; they are silent about it, and the silence is filled when the abstract Hilbert space is identified with the physical one.
