Why does nature obey n = 1 (single tensor product \|ψ⟩⟨ψ\|, Born rule \|⟨ϕ\|ψ⟩\|²) rather than n = 2 (double tensor product \|ψ⟩⟨ψ\|\^⊗2, alternative rule \|⟨ϕ\|ψ⟩\|⁴)? ##### 7.1.9.B The asymmetric depth test

A foundational derivation has to bottom out somewhere, and the question is *where*. Three terminating points are available in the reconstruction tradition: operational axioms about measurement outcomes, mathematical axioms about Hilbert spaces, and physical principles about what nature does. Masanes–Galley–Müller bottom out at the operational layer; von Neumann’s 1932 axiomatization bottoms out at the mathematical layer; the McGucken Principle bottoms out at the physical layer. Each layer is foundational relative to the layer above and derived relative to the layer below.

The clean test for which derivation is more foundational is reciprocal: ask each framework to derive the *inputs* of the other.

**Can McGucken derive Masanes–Galley–Müller’s six inputs?** Yes, all six. The complex Hilbert space is L²(Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$, dμ_M), the function space on the constraint surface where dx₄/dt = ic holds locally (Theorem 6.1, completed by Cauchy completion of the pre-Hilbert space 𝓥 of complex amplitudes over Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$). Unitarity is x₄-flux conservation: the evolution U(t) = exp(−iĤt/ℏ) preserves the Born inner product because it preserves the total x₄-projection density across the spatial slice (Theorem 9.2). The tensor-product structure for composite systems is Fubini–Tonelli on independent x₄-expansions from causally independent source events: L²(M\^{(A)}*{1,3} × M\^{(B)}*{1,3}, dμ\^{(A)}*M ⊗ dμ\^{(B)}*M) ≅ L²(M\^{(A)}*{1,3}, dμ\^{(A)}*M) ⊗ L²(M\^{(B)}*{1,3}, dμ\^{(B)}*M) (Corollary 11.6). The OPF formalism is the operational shadow of projections of x₄-advance onto the spatial slice — each OPF f(ψ) is, in the McGucken reading, the density of x₄-projection at a localized apparatus event evaluated on the McGucken Sphere 𝓜_E(t). ⋆-product associativity is the associativity of independent x₄-expansion tensor structure on the constraint surface, derived from Fubini–Tonelli on three independent x₄-expansions: the probability that three causally independent sources A, B, C jointly produce an outcome cannot depend on whether we describe them as (A · B) · C or A · (B · C), because both descriptions correspond to the same physical x₄-expansion configuration on M\^{(A)}*{1,3} × M\^{(B)}*{1,3} × M\^{(C)}\_{1,3}. Finite-parameter state estimation holds because the SU(d) adjoint representation N\^d_1 = the operator algebra on the McGucken Sphere has finite dimension d² − 1, and the spacetime constraint surface Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ is 3+1-dimensional with finite-dimensional Hilbert-space restriction on any bounded support.

All six Masanes–Galley–Müller inputs are derived from the single McGucken input. The derivation is complete and theorem-by-theorem.

**Can Masanes–Galley–Müller derive McGucken’s one input?** No. Masanes–Galley–Müller cannot derive dx₄/dt = ic from operational axioms about measurement outcomes, because operational axioms are silent on the geometric structure of spacetime. The Masanes–Galley–Müller framework has no language for *what is the fourth dimension doing*. The OPF formalism describes what an observer sees when measuring a system; it cannot describe the physical structure that causes the observer to see what they see. There is no path from “outcome probability functions on ℙℂ\^d satisfy closure properties (7-9)” to “the fourth dimension is expanding at the velocity of light from every spacetime event.” The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic lies entirely outside Masanes–Galley–Müller’s expressive vocabulary.

The derivation relation is therefore asymmetric: McGucken → Masanes–Galley–Müller is a complete cascade through Theorems 6.1, 9.2, and Corollary 11.6; Masanes–Galley–Müller → McGucken is empty. This asymmetry is the formal test of foundational depth. The dx₄/dt = ic framework whose inputs can be derived from the other’s inputs is the less foundational of the two. The dx₄/dt = ic framework whose inputs *cannot* be derived from the other’s inputs is the more foundational. By this test the McGucken Principle is more foundational than the Masanes–Galley–Müller postulates by a clear margin.

##### 7.1.9.C The architectural question

A second, complementary test asks what each framework identifies as the central structure in its own derivation — the specific component that, if removed, causes the entire derivation to fail.

Theorem 18 of the paper proves that for n ≥ 2 no associative ⋆-product on M\^a_n × M\^b_n → M\^ab_n exists; the proof uses the (n−1,1) Young tableau, the Schur–Weyl decomposition under SU(a) ⊗ SU(b), and Lemma 16’s Littlewood–Richardson rule. The Born rule (n = 1) survives only because for n = 1 the contradiction does not arise (W\^b_illicit is trivially empty when λ = μ = (1)). Drop associativity, and the §III.A toy theory with n = 2 — where states are represented by \|ψ⟩⟨ψ\|\^⊗2 and probabilities by tr\[F\|ψ⟩⟨ψ\|\^⊗2\] — becomes admissible. Associativity is the central algebraic requirement of the entire Masanes–Galley–Müller derivation.

The Masanes–Galley–Müller framework does not derive associativity. It is postulated as axiom (14) and accepted as a basic feature of the ⋆-product on the grounds that “deciding to describe a tripartite system A · B · C as either the bipartite system AB · C or as A · BC must not modify the outcome probabilities.” This is presented as a self-evident operational requirement — but operational self-evidence is not derivation. *Why* should descriptions invariant under regrouping correspond to the same outcome probabilities? Masanes–Galley–Müller provide no physical reason.

The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic integrates to x₄ = ict, and the Euclidean line element on ambient four-dimensional space restricts to the Minkowski metric on the constraint surface Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ via (ict)² = −c²t² (Lemma 2.5). This metric is rank 2: bilinear in two arguments dx\^μ and dx\^ν, with ds² = g_μν dx\^μ dx\^ν being the canonical rank-2 form. The Born density is the rank-2 metric pairing of the forward x₄-expansion (carrying ict-phase, ψ) with the conjugate x₄-expansion (carrying −ict-phase, ψ*) on the McGucken Sphere 𝓜_E(t) at the apparatus event: P = ψ*ψ = \|ψ\|² (Theorem 7.2). The rank-2 character directly forces n = 1 in the Masanes–Galley–Müller classification: bilinear pairing in (ψ, ψ\*) corresponds to n = 1 (single tensor product \|ψ⟩⟨ψ\|, squared modulus), while a rank-4 pairing would correspond to n = 2 (double tensor product \|ψ⟩⟨ψ\|\^⊗2, Aaronson’s \|⟨ϕᵢ\|ψ⟩\|⁴ rule from arXiv:quant-ph/0401062).

The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework derives associativity. The associativity of the ⋆-product is the associativity of independent x₄-expansion tensor structure on the constraint surface, and it is forced by Fubini–Tonelli on three independent x₄-expansions: the order of tensor products of independent function spaces is associative, so the order of descriptions of independent sources is too. The *physical reason* associativity holds — which Masanes–Galley–Müller cannot supply — is that three causally independent x₄-expansions from three independent source events combine into a single product structure on M\^{(A)}*{1,3} × M\^{(B)}*{1,3} × M\^{(C)}\_{1,3} regardless of how the bracketing is chosen. Associativity is a derived geometric fact.

The contrast: Masanes–Galley–Müller’s associativity is postulated and the squared modulus is derived from it; McGucken’s rank-2 metric is derived from the McGucken Principle and the squared modulus is derived from the metric, with associativity itself derived as a downstream geometric fact. The McGucken derivation goes one level deeper: it identifies *what physical structure makes associativity true*, which Masanes–Galley–Müller leave unexplained.

##### 7.1.9.D The Schrödinger 1926 test

There is a historical test that pins down what “foundational” means at the foundational level. On 6 June 1926, Erwin Schrödinger wrote to H. A. Lorentz: *“What is unpleasant here, and indeed directly to be objected to, is the use of complex numbers. Ψ is surely fundamentally a real function.”* (Quoted in Einstein–Przibram–Klein, *Letters on Wave Mechanics*, 2011; cited as reference \[3\] in Renou et al. 2021.) This is the canonical statement of the foundational complaint about the Born rule and its complex amplitudes, formulated within months of Schrödinger’s own publication of the wave equation. The complaint is precise: Schrödinger objects that the complex character of ψ has *no physical referent* in the dx₄/dt = ic framework he has just published. The ψ-function appears in his derivation as a mathematical construct by analogy with Hamilton–Jacobi theory; the complex numbers entered as a computational convenience rather than as a description of any physical structure. Schrödinger himself concluded by 1928 that ψ was not to be interpreted as a physical wave at all.

What would a *foundational* answer to Schrödinger 1926 look like? It would have to identify what physical structure the complex amplitudes refer to — what element of reality the imaginary unit i in ψ describes. Anything short of this leaves Schrödinger’s complaint open. The Renou et al. (2021) experimental result (§6.2.22) provides the empirical pillar: complex numbers are necessary, real-vector-space alternatives are experimentally excluded. But Renou himself acknowledges the explanatory gap: *“the early founders of quantum mechanics could not find any way to interpret the complex numbers appearing in the theory. Having them worked very well, but there is no clear way to identify the complex numbers with an element of reality”* (Renou interview, *Live Science*, December 2021). Renou’s experimental result confirms *that* complex numbers are physically necessary; it does not explain *what physical fact* the complex numbers describe.

The Masanes–Galley–Müller framework begins with Postulate (states): *“To every physical system there corresponds a complex and separable Hilbert space ℂ\^d.”* The complex Hilbert space is the foundational input, accepted without derivation. The Masanes–Galley–Müller theorem then shows that given this complex Hilbert space and the other operational postulates, the Born rule emerges as the unique probability rule. But Schrödinger’s complaint was precisely about the complex character of the Hilbert space. Asked *why complex numbers*, Masanes–Galley–Müller’s answer is in effect: *because if you accept the complex Hilbert space as foundational, the Born rule is the unique probability rule consistent with operational axioms*. This is not an answer to Schrödinger’s question. It is a re-statement of the premise Schrödinger was objecting to. The Masanes–Galley–Müller derivation is foundationally silent on Schrödinger 1926 because the complex character of the Hilbert space is *upstream* of where Masanes–Galley–Müller begin.

The complex numbers in ψ are the algebraic signature of the perpendicular fourth dimension x₄. The imaginary unit i is the geometric marker for the one perpendicular axis beyond x₁x₂x₃, with x₄ = ict being the integrated coordinate shadow of dx₄/dt = ic. ψ(x, t) is the projection of x₄-advance from a worldline event onto the spatial location x at time t — a complex amplitude because x₄-advance carries phase from the imaginary-unit factor of x₄ = ict. The element of reality the complex amplitudes describe is the expanding fourth dimension perpendicular to ordinary 3-space, advancing at rate c with action ℏ per Planck-frequency oscillation. Schrödinger 1926 was correct that the complex character of ψ requires a physical referent; he was correct that his own derivation of ψ from Hamilton–Jacobi analogy did not supply one; and he was correct to be uncomfortable with treating ψ as fundamental without that referent in hand. The McGucken Principle supplies what Schrödinger could not — the referent that justifies the complex character of ψ.

The historical force of this test is sharp. Schrödinger himself, the originator of the wave equation, identified the complex character of ψ as the foundational puzzle within weeks of his own publication. He could not solve it and abandoned the physical interpretation of ψ by 1928. The puzzle has persisted in the foundations literature for nearly a century, through Gleason (1957), Mackey (1957), Piron (1964), Solèr (1995), Hardy (2001), Chiribella–D’Ariano–Perinotti (2010s), Masanes–Galley–Müller (2019), Renou et al. (2021), and beyond. Each of these programs operates *inside* the complex Hilbert space and derives various consequences from it; none has been able to identify the physical referent of the imaginary unit i. The Renou et al. experiment closes the empirical route by showing the complex numbers are physically necessary; the Renou framing of the open question — *“there is no clear way to identify the complex numbers with an element of reality”* — confirms that the philosophical puzzle is still open at the foundational layer. The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic answers it: the element of reality is x₄, perpendicular to x₁x₂x₃, expanding at rate c.

Masanes–Galley–Müller derive the Born rule given a postulated complex Hilbert space and five operational axioms; McGucken derives the Born rule together with the complex Hilbert space and all the operational structure, all from a single physical principle about the active expansion of the fourth dimension at the velocity of light. The Masanes–Galley–Müller derivation is rigorous and impressive within the operational reconstruction tradition; the McGucken derivation is foundational in the sense Schrödinger 1926 asked for — it identifies what physical structure the formalism describes. The architectural ratio is six postulates to one principle. The asymmetric depth test is unambiguous: McGucken can derive all six Masanes–Galley–Müller inputs as downstream theorems, and Masanes–Galley–Müller cannot derive the McGucken Principle from operational axioms because operational axioms are silent on the geometric structure of spacetime. The contrast is precise: Masanes–Galley–Müller’s central axiom is associativity (postulated), while McGucken’s central structure is the rank-2 metric (derived from the McGucken Principle), with associativity itself derived from Fubini–Tonelli on independent x₄-expansions. The Schrödinger 1926 historical test is decisive: McGucken answers the question Schrödinger asked; Masanes–Galley–Müller cannot, because the complex Hilbert space stands as the foundational primitive of Masanes–Galley–Müller’s framework and the question of *what physical structure makes it complex* lies entirely upstream of Masanes–Galley–Müller’s expressive layer.

Foundational depth is measured by *where the derivation bottoms out*; both derivations are rigorous in their own layer. Masanes–Galley–Müller bottom out in operational primitives about measurement and probability on a postulated complex Hilbert space. McGucken bottoms out in a physical statement about the active expansion of the fourth dimension. The difference is the difference between deriving the Born rule from the structure of measurement and deriving the Born rule from the structure of spacetime itself. Schrödinger 1926 was asking for the latter. McGucken supplies it.

The Born rule is derived from Dutch-book coherence — an agent assigning quantum probabilities other than \|ψ\|² would be subject to a sure-loss betting strategy.

#### 7.1.15 Schlosshauer–Fine (2005) critical review

Maximilian Schlosshauer and Arthur Fine’s “On Zurek’s Derivation of the Born Rule” (*Foundations of Physics* 35, 197–213, 2005) gave a critical review of Zurek’s envariance derivation, identifying tacit assumptions and arguing that the derivation, while not strictly circular, requires additional premises that themselves need justification.

*McGucken diagnostic.* Schlosshauer and Fine’s critical analysis is representative of the broader skeptical literature on Born-rule derivations (Barnum et al. 2000, Saunders 2004, Gill 2005, Lewis 2010, Hemmo–Pitowsky 2007, Rae 2009, Dawid–Thébault 2014). The critical consensus is that *no* derivation of the Born rule from the other postulates of quantum theory succeeds without additional assumptions whose physical origin is unexplained. This consensus is the diagnostic background that makes the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework’s upstream derivation necessary: the only way to derive the rule is from a principle upstream of the formalism, which is what dx₄/dt = ic supplies.

#### 7.1.16 POVM generalization and operational-detector programs (Davies–Lewis 1970, Neumaier 2025)

Edward Brian Davies and John T. Lewis introduced the positive operator-valued measure (POVM) generalization of the Born rule in 1970 (“An Operational Approach to Quantum Probability,” *Communications in Mathematical Physics* 17, 239–260). The motivation was that real quantum measurements — measurements with finite detector efficiency, dark counts, losses, decoherence in the apparatus, the simultaneous low-resolution measurement of position and momentum, and outcomes that do not coincide with eigenvalues of the measured observable — cannot be described by projection-valued measures. The POVM is the mathematical structure that captures real measurements: a family of positive operators {P_k} summing to the identity, with the probability of outcome k given by tr(ρ P_k). By the 1990s the POVM form had become standard in quantum optics and quantum information theory (Nielsen and Chuang \[117\]; Busch, Lahti, and Werner \[105\]). The relation between POVM and projective forms is Naimark’s dilation theorem (Mark Naimark 1940): every POVM on a Hilbert space 𝓗 lifts to a projection-valued measure on a larger Hilbert space 𝓗 ⊗ 𝒦 obtained by tensoring with an ancilla space, and the projective Born rule on the dilated space reproduces the POVM rule on the original space.

Arnold Neumaier’s “The Born rule – 100 years ago and today” (arXiv:2502.08545v3, March 2025) surveys ten distinct historical formulations of the Born rule (universal/projective, discrete spectral, finite spectral, scattering objective, scattering measurement, objective, measurement, POVM, condensed, and quantum-statistical-mechanics forms), and proposes a derivation of the POVM form from what he calls the Detector Response Principle (DRP). The DRP defines what a “quantum measurement device” is by listing its operational properties — detection elements labeled by a finite set K, response rates, stationarity of the source, and the relation between mean rates and the density operator of the source — and Neumaier proves a Detector Response Theorem (\[Neumaier–Westra 2024, §4.1.2\]) yielding a unique POVM {P_k} characterizing the device’s response. The POVM Born rule then falls out as a theorem. The program is developed at length in Neumaier’s books *Coherent Quantum Physics* (Cambridge University Press, 2019) and Neumaier–Westra’s *Algebraic Quantum Physics, Vol. 1* (2024).

*McGucken diagnostic.* Theorem 7.2 of the present paper derives the *projective* Born rule P = \|ψ\|² — the form Born stated in 1926 (\[8, 9\]), the form in every textbook, and the form whose architectural inversion-to-corollary is the central derivational claim. The POVM generalization is recoverable in the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework via Naimark dilation: the McGucken Hilbert space 𝓗 of Theorem 6.1 admits ancilla tensor extensions 𝓗 ⊗ 𝒦, and the projective Born rule on the dilated space reproduces the POVM rule on 𝓗. The architectural inversion of the present paper — from postulated Born rule to forced theorem of dx₄/dt = ic — carries to the POVM form by this dilation, with the McGucken Sphere expansion in the dilated space supplying the rank-2 metric pairing that grounds (R4) in the larger setting.

The deeper diagnostic concerns what the operational-detector programs actually import to do their derivational work. Davies–Lewis 1970 is a *technical generalization* that takes the entire Hilbert-space formalism as given and extends the Born rule from projections to positive operator–valued measures. It postulates nothing foundational; it generalizes within the existing formalism. The POVM structure itself is the postulate, on top of standard quantum mechanics.

Neumaier 2025 is a derivation, but the postulate it starts from — the DRP — is not a single physical principle. The phrase “Detector Response Principle” sounds like one principle. It functions as an *entire measurement-physics ontology* compressed into an operational definition. Reading the DRP as it is actually stated, the program postulates: (i) the Hilbert space 𝓗 on which the density operator ρ acts (imported silently from standard quantum mechanics); (ii) the density operator formalism itself, with the trace pairing tr(ρ A) as the value functional on operators; (iii) time as a parameter of evolution, required to define mean rates; (iv) stationarity of the source as an operational stability condition; (v) the existence of discrete detection events as the primitive ontology of outcomes; (vi) the existence of detection elements labeled by a finite set K as an a priori partition of outcome space; (vii) the pairing of detection elements with the source via operators P_k; and (viii) the operational notion of a “quantum measurement device” as a primitive concept. Each of these is foundational machinery imported into the DRP, not derived by it. The “one principle” framing obscures that the DRP is doing the work of eight foundational commitments — comparable in foundational content to Masanes–Galley–Müller’s six measurement axioms or to the suite of assumptions in the operational reconstructions of Hardy (§7.1.12) and Chiribella–D’Ariano–Perinotti (§7.1.12). The DRP is honest about deriving the POVM Born rule from itself; it is not honest about how much it imports along the way.

The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework derives all eight of the DRP’s imported commitments from upstream geometry. The Hilbert space 𝓗 is constructed (Theorem 6.1) as the Cauchy completion of the space of x₄-projections, not assumed. The density operator formalism is the standard convex-combination structure on 𝓗 (Corollary 11.1). Time is the parameter of x₄-advance (the McGucken Principle itself supplies the time direction via dx₄/dt). Detection events are the geometric incidence of forward and conjugate x₄-expansions on a localized absorber (Theorem 7.4). The “detector” is, in the McGucken reading, a region of spacetime where x₄-expansion is locally absorbed by a macroscopic apparatus with definite x₄-localization (Theorem 7.4, measurement-as-meeting-of-two-expansions). The operational notion of a “quantum measurement device” is a derived structure: it is whatever physical assembly produces detection events as geometric overlaps of two expansions. The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework is the only program in the present literature survey that derives *both* the detector and the rule from a principle upstream of both. This is the architectural inversion in its full form: derived measurement ontology in place of postulated measurement ontology, all descending from dx₄/dt = ic.

In the simplicity-of-foundational-commitment ranking, Davies–Lewis and Neumaier therefore land at different positions. Davies–Lewis is roughly equivalent to Born 1926 — it states (or generalizes) the rule on top of the existing Hilbert-space formalism without deriving anything foundational. Neumaier’s DRP-based derivation is more ambitious but imports an eight-fold suite of operational commitments under the label of a single “principle.” The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic, by contrast, is a single physical equation about geometric flow — five symbols, one action-quantization clause — from which the Hilbert space, the density operator structure, the time parameter, the detection-event ontology, and the projective Born rule are all derived as theorems, with the POVM generalization recoverable via Naimark dilation.

#### 7.1.17 Diagnostic across all sixteen programs

The pattern is uniform across all sixteen programs: every prior derivation operates *inside* the Hilbert-space formalism (or, in the case of Davies–Lewis and Neumaier, *inside* an even larger operational-detector formalism that imports the Hilbert space and adds detector-ontological structure on top), and imports a supplementary axiom — a probability measure on subspaces, a rationality axiom, an environment-induced symmetry, an equivariant measure, a self-locating uncertainty principle, a branch-counting principle, a Dutch-book coherence requirement, an operational/informational axiom, a logical-inference axiom, or a detector-response principle — whose content is essentially the Born measure (or the detector ontology that already pre-supposes the Born measure) already, dressed in the language of the program. The critical literature has consistently identified this as the pattern.

The McGucken diagnostic identifies the upstream geometric source these programs could not see: P = \|ψ\|² is the unique density satisfying (R1)–(R4), with each requirement supplied by one foundational feature of dx₄/dt = ic:

-   (R1) Reality — descends from the physical meaning of probability as frequency of detection events (universal feature).
-   (R2) Non-negativity — descends from the same.
-   (R3) Phase invariance — descends from the universality of x₄-expansion from every event (universal x₄-shift is unobservable).
-   (R4) Bilinearity in (ψ, ψ\*) — descends from the rank-2 character of the Minkowski metric induced by x₄ = ict, which is the central geometric fact of the derivation.

No prior program had R4 derived from upstream physics — every program either stipulated bilinearity as an axiom (Hardy, Chiribella–D’Ariano–Perinotti, Masanes–Müller) or extracted it from operational redundancies (Masanes–Galley–Müller) or showed it was forced by additional axioms (Gleason). The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework derives R4 from the rank-2 structure of the Minkowski metric, which is itself derived from (ict)² = −c² t², which is the integrated coordinate shadow of dx₄/dt = ic. The Born rule is therefore not an axiom, and not a result of agent rationality or self-locating uncertainty: it is a forced geometric theorem of one physical principle.

### 7.2 The McGucken strategy for the Born rule: derive P(x) = \|ψ(x)\|² as the unique density satisfying four requirements (reality, non-negativity, phase-invariance, bilinearity in (ψ,ψ\*)), all four forced by the geometry of dx₄/dt = ic

The McGucken derivation operates one level upstream. ψ is constructed (Definition 2.6) as the projection of x₄-advance onto the spatial slice. The Hilbert space is constructed (Theorem 6.1) as the L² completion of the space of such projections. The Born density is then the unique density on this pre-Hilbert structure compatible with four physical requirements descending from dx₄/dt = ic.

### 7.3 The four requirements (R1)–(R4) for the Born density forced by dx₄/dt = ic: R1 reality from real probability interpretation; R2 non-negativity from probability axiom; R3 phase invariance from global x₄-advance gauge freedom; R4 bilinearity in (ψ,ψ\*) from rank-2 character of Lorentzian metric (Lemma 7.1)

A probability density P on ℝ³ derived from the McGucken wavefunction ψ must satisfy:

-   **(R1) Reality.** $P(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}$. (Probabilities are real numbers.)
-   **(R2) Non-negativity.** $P(\mathbf{x}) \geq 0$. (Probabilities are non-negative.)
-   **(R3) Phase invariance under global x₄-shift.** P(e\^iα ψ) = P(ψ) for all α ∈ ℝ. (A global phase is a homogeneous shift of the x₄-origin, geometrically unobservable because the McGucken expansion is universal from every event.)
-   \*\*(R4) Bilinearity in (ψ, ψ\^\*).\*\* P is a bilinear function of ψ and ψ\^*. (The probability density at B ∈ 𝓜_E(t) is the geometric overlap of the forward x₄-advance with its conjugate at B; this overlap is the metric pairing of the four-velocity along the forward advance with the four-velocity along the conjugate. The Minkowski metric induced by x₄ = ict via (ict)² = −c² t² is a rank-2 tensor on the four-velocity: the pairing is bilinear in its two arguments by the definition of a rank-2 tensor. Lifting to amplitude representation gives bilinearity in (ψ, ψ\^*). Higher-order forms are excluded because the metric structure is rank 2.)

Each requirement is supplied by the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic and the Sphere geometry it generates. All four requirements are forced by specific Sphere properties; none is imported as a separate probability axiom.

*(R1) Reality* is forced by the geometric meaning of $\psi^* \psi$ as Sphere overlap and equivalently as the head-on collision rate of two McGucken Spheres at the detection event. By Theorem 7.4 (below), the Born density at a spatial-slice point B is the geometric overlap of the forward x₄-expansion with the conjugate x₄-expansion at B — a real-valued geometric quantity by construction, as the simultaneous evaluation of two complex-conjugate path-integral kernels at the same spacetime point reduces to $K^*(B,A)\, K(B,A) = |K(B,A)|^2 \in \mathbb{R}$. By Theorem 7.7 (below), the same density is the local rate of head-on collisions between two physical McGucken Spheres (emitter’s and absorber’s) at the detection event — a count of discrete physical events per unit time per unit spatial volume, hence intrinsically real-valued. R1 is therefore a forced consequence of the Sphere’s geometric role as the source of detection events.

*(R2) Non-negativity* is forced by the same Sphere-geometric grounding. By Theorem 7.7, the head-on collision rate of two Spheres counts physical events, and an event count cannot be negative. By Theorem 7.4, the Sphere-overlap density $\psi^* \psi = |\psi|^2$ is non-negative as the squared modulus of a complex amplitude. By Theorem 7.11 (below), the free-propagation reading $|\psi(P,t)|^2 = \psi(P, t) \cdot \psi(PT_E \cdot (P, t))$ is the multiplication of a wavefunction value with its PT-symmetric partner, with the result being the squared modulus by the symmetry identity $\psi(PT_E \cdot \text{event}) = \psi^*(\text{event})$ — again non-negative by construction. R2 is therefore Sphere-geometric, not a separately postulated probability axiom.

*(R3) Phase invariance under global x₄-shift* is forced by the universality clause of dx₄/dt = ic. By Theorem 2.4 clause (iv), every spacetime event has its own McGucken Sphere expansion at +ic, with the wavefront assignment $\Sigma_M : p \mapsto \Sigma^+(p)$ translation-invariant by the universality of the McGucken Principle. A global phase $e^{i\alpha}$ applied to ψ corresponds to shifting all action contributions $S[\gamma]$ in the path-integral kernel $\psi(B) = \sum_\gamma \exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$ by the constant $\hbar\alpha$, which by Proposition 2.2’s action-quantization clause corresponds to a global shift of the x₄-origin. Because every event already has its own Sphere expansion at +ic and the assignment is universal, the x₄-origin is intrinsically arbitrary and a global shift is geometrically unobservable. R3 is therefore Sphere-geometric — forced by the universality clause of dx₄/dt = ic — not a separately postulated symmetry axiom.

*(R4) Bilinearity in $(\psi, \psi^*)$* is forced by the rank-2 character of the Minkowski metric $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ supplied by Lemma 2.5, with the rank-2 character itself being a forced consequence of $(ic)^2 = -c^2$ — the squared form of dx₄/dt = ic. The probability density at $B \in \mathcal{M}_E(t)$ is the geometric overlap of the forward x₄-advance with its conjugate at B; this overlap is the metric pairing of the four-velocity along the forward advance with the four-velocity along the conjugate. The Minkowski metric induced by $x_4 = ict$ via $(ict)^2 = -c^2 t^2$ is a rank-2 tensor on the four-velocity: the pairing is bilinear in its two arguments by the definition of a rank-2 tensor. Lifting to amplitude representation gives bilinearity in $(\psi, \psi^*)$; higher-order forms (rank-4 quartic densities such as Aaronson’s $|\psi|^4 / \sum_j |\psi_j|^4$) are excluded by the rank-counting argument of Lemma 7.1 (below). The specific *product* form $\psi \cdot \psi^*$ is forced by two derived ingredients of Lemma 7.7.5: (a) the action-additivity argument (Step 1) — independent McGucken-Sphere paths have additive actions $S_{\text{joint}} = S_A + S_B$, hence multiplicative amplitudes $\psi_{\text{joint}} = \psi_A \cdot \psi_B$, ruling out sum, max, min, arithmetic/geometric/harmonic means; and (b) the complexification argument (Step 2) — the symmetric rank-2 metric $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ admits exactly two complex extensions (bilinear and sesquilinear), and R1 (real Born density on diagonal) forces the sesquilinear extension with conjugation. R4 is therefore Sphere-geometric and grade **G1 within v46** — fully derived from rank-2 metric symmetry (Lemma 2.5) plus complex-valued wavefunction (Theorem 3.1) plus action-additivity (Step 1 of Lemma 7.7.5) plus complexification + R1 (Step 2 of Lemma 7.7.5), not a separately postulated bilinearity assumption and not asserted by “elementary collision kinematics.” The conjugation in $\psi^* \psi$ is the conjugation of the sesquilinear complexification — neither a Lorentz boost (the action $S$ is a Lorentz scalar, so $\exp(iS/\hbar)$ is frame-invariant) nor a postulated Stueckelberg–Feynman time-reversal identification, but the unique complex extension of the symmetric rank-2 metric consistent with real Born density.

All four requirements R1–R4 therefore descend from McGucken Sphere properties: Sphere overlap and head-on collision as detection-event source (R1, R2), Sphere universality across all spacetime events (R3), and rank-2 metric on the Sphere wavefront (R4). The Born rule is in this sense **fully geometric** — every condition entering Theorem 7.2’s uniqueness derivation traces to a specific Sphere property, with no probability axiom imported as separate input.

### 7.4 Lemma 7.1: bilinearity of x₄-flux — the rank-2 character of the Minkowski metric g_μν inherited from (ict)² = -c²t² forces sesquilinearity of the natural ψ/ψ\* pairing on the McGucken Sphere

**Lemma 7.1 (Bilinearity of x₄-flux).** *Let ψ be the McGucken wavefunction of Definition 2.6, taking values on the spatial slice ℝ³ at parameter time t. Then any density P(x, t) on ℝ³ that arises as the natural metric pairing of ψ with its conjugate ψ\^* on the McGucken Sphere 𝓜_E(t) is sesquilinear in ψ — bilinear in the pair (ψ, ψ\^*), with the bilinearity inherited from the rank-2 character of the Minkowski metric g_μν induced by x₄ = ict.*

*Proof.* By Lemma 2.5, the constraint surface carries the Minkowski metric g_μν with signature (-, +, +, +), generated by the substitution dx₄² = (ic)² dt² = −c² dt². The metric is a rank-2 tensor: it pairs two vectors and produces a scalar, with the pairing g_μν A\^μ B\^ν bilinear in (A, B) by definition.

We construct the natural bilinear pairing of ψ with ψ\^\* that the rank-2 metric supplies. By Theorem 3.1, ψ is the path-integral kernel ψ(B) = ∑\_γ exp(i S\[γ\]/ℏ) from the source event E to the spacetime point B, propagated by the forward x₄-expansion (carrying phase factor from x₄ = ict). The conjugate wavefunction ψ\^\*(B) = ∑\_γ exp(-i S\[γ\]/ℏ) is the same path-sum with reversed phase, equivalently the path-integral kernel propagated by the *conjugate* x₄-coordinate x₄\^\* = -ict (Definition 7.3 of the main paper). The conjugate is the same flow read in opposite orientation; the algebraic operation ψ ↦ ψ\^\* records this reversal.

A natural metric pairing of ψ with ψ\^\* at the spacetime point B is the product ψ\^*(B) ψ(B) — the simultaneous evaluation of the forward and conjugate kernels at B, which is the geometry of “the two expansions meet at B” (this content is made explicit in Theorem 7.4 below as the geometric meaning of the Born rule). This pairing is, by construction, bilinear in (ψ, ψ\^*): linear in ψ in one slot, linear in ψ\^\* in the other. The bilinearity is therefore inherited from the rank-2 metric structure: the rank-2 metric admits a unique-up-to-scalar natural bilinear pairing of forward and conjugate path-sums on the McGucken Sphere, and any density derived from this pairing is bilinear in (ψ, ψ\^\*).

Higher-rank metric pairings — rank-4 forms such as g_μνρσ A\^μ A\^ν B\^ρ B\^σ — would give quartic densities such as (ψ\^\* ψ)² or \|ψ\|⁴ / ∑\_j \|ψ_j\|⁴ (Aaronson’s alternative rule, ref. \[40\] of Masanes–Galley–Müller). These are excluded by the rank-2 character of the metric g_μν that x₄ = ict supplies. The Minkowski metric is rank-2, not rank-4 or higher; the natural pairing on (ψ, ψ\^\*) is therefore bilinear, not quartic. ∎

**Lemma 7.1.5 (Uniqueness of the SO(3)-invariant probability measure on the McGucken Sphere).** *The McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p)$ at parameter time $t$ is a round 2-sphere $S^2$ of radius $ct$, carrying the transitive action of the rotation group $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ fixed by the isotropy of the $x_4$-expansion from $p$ (clause 3 of §2.4). Then there exists a unique $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-invariant Borel probability measure on the Sphere, namely the normalized round measure $d\mu(\theta,\phi) = \sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi/(4\pi)$, and every $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-invariant probability density on the Sphere is this $d\mu$. This is the measure that supplies the Born-rule probability over detection directions.*

*Proof.* The Sphere is a homogeneous space for $\mathrm{SO}(3)$: the isotropy of the expansion makes the action transitive, and the stabilizer of any direction is the subgroup $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ of rotations about that axis, so $\Sigma_+(p) \cong \mathrm{SO}(3)/\mathrm{SO}(2) = S^2$. $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is compact; by Haar’s theorem (1933) every compact group carries a unique normalized invariant measure, which pushes forward to a unique invariant probability measure on any homogeneous space. Existence: $d\mu = \sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi/(4\pi)$ is invariant because rotations are isometries of the round metric and $\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi$ is its area element. Uniqueness: if $\nu$ is any $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-invariant probability measure, then for continuous $f$, invariance plus transitivity give $\int f\,d\nu = \int f\,d\mu$ (both equal the round average $\bar f$); since this holds for all continuous $f$, $\nu = \mu$ by the Riesz representation theorem. The corresponding result \[MG-Symmetry\] Theorem 22.6 develops the same uniqueness in the correlation setting; the self-contained statement is the one given here. $\blacksquare$

*Remark 7.1.5a (Why this is the measure the Born rule needs).* A probability rule over outcomes requires a measure on the outcome space, and a measure is physically forced only if a symmetry singles it out uniquely. Minkowski’s four-velocity norm $u^\mu u_\mu = -c^2$ carries no group action and hence no distinguished measure; the McGucken Sphere carries the transitive $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ action, and Lemma 7.1.5 shows this action forces exactly one probability measure. The Born-rule weight over detection directions is that measure. This is the route to $P = |\psi|^2$ that proceeds from the Sphere’s *symmetry group*, independently of the route that proceeds from the Sphere’s *metric rank* (Lemma 7.1).

**Lemma 7.6 (Parallelogram identity from rank-2 sesquilinear character — McGucken-internal).** *Let ⟨·, ·⟩ : 𝓥 × 𝓥 → ℂ be the rank-2 sesquilinear inner product on the McGucken pre-Hilbert space 𝓥 supplied by Lemma 7.1 (rank-2 character inherited from (ict)² = −c² t² of Lemma 2.5, equivalently from dx₄/dt = ic). Let ‖ψ‖ := √⟨ψ, ψ⟩ be the associated norm. Then for all x, y ∈ 𝓥, the parallelogram identity*

$\|x + y\|^2 + \|x - y\|^2 = 2(\|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2)$

*holds as a direct two-line algebraic consequence of the rank-2 sesquilinearity of ⟨·, ·⟩ — without invocation of the Jordan–von Neumann theorem or any external functional-analytic input. The parallelogram identity is therefore a McGucken-internal consequence of dx₄/dt = ic via Lemma 2.5 and Lemma 7.1.*

*Proof.* By the rank-2 sesquilinearity of ⟨·, ·⟩ (conjugate-linear in the first slot, linear in the second), direct expansion gives

$\|x + y\|^2 = \langle x + y, x + y\rangle = \langle x, x\rangle + \langle x, y\rangle + \langle y, x\rangle + \langle y, y\rangle = \|x\|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}\langle x, y\rangle + \|y\|^2,$

$\|x - y\|^2 = \langle x - y, x - y\rangle = \langle x, x\rangle - \langle x, y\rangle - \langle y, x\rangle + \langle y, y\rangle = \|x\|^2 - 2\operatorname{Re}\langle x, y\rangle + \|y\|^2,$

using ⟨y, x⟩ = ⟨x, y⟩\* (conjugate symmetry of the McGucken inner product, established in §6.4 from the complex-conjugation under the integral sign in ⟨φ, ψ⟩ = ∫φ\*ψ d³x) so that ⟨x, y⟩ + ⟨y, x⟩ = 2 Re⟨x, y⟩. Adding the two expansions and observing that the cross-terms ±2 Re⟨x, y⟩ cancel:

$\|x + y\|^2 + \|x - y\|^2 = 2\|x\|^2 + 2\|y\|^2 = 2(\|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2). \square$

The parallelogram identity is therefore a *direct two-line algebraic consequence* of the rank-2 sesquilinear character of the inner product supplied by Lemma 7.1, which itself descends from the rank-2 character of the Minkowski metric (Lemma 2.5), which descends from (ict)² = −c² t² — the squared form of dx₄/dt = ic. The McGucken framework supplies the parallelogram identity through the cascade dx₄/dt = ic → (ict)² = −c² t² → Lorentzian metric → rank-2 sesquilinear inner product → parallelogram identity, with all intermediate steps internal to the dx₄/dt = ic framework.

The Jordan–von Neumann theorem (1935) \[123\] gives the converse direction — that any norm satisfying the parallelogram identity arises from an inner product — and is the historical functional-analytic statement of the forward-and-converse equivalence. In the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework, the converse direction is unnecessary as upstream input: the inner product is supplied directly by Lemma 7.1, and the parallelogram identity follows by Lemma 7.6 as a downstream consequence. Jordan–von Neumann therefore serves as a *downstream consistency check* (confirming that the McGucken-derived parallelogram-identity structure is consistent with general functional analysis on L\^p spaces) rather than as an upstream selection principle. The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework derives the L² character of 𝓗 from the rank-2 metric directly; Jordan–von Neumann confirms this is consistent with the broader L\^p classification but is no longer used as foundational input.

### 7.5 Theorem 7.2 (Born rule from dx₄/dt = ic): the unique density on ℝ³ satisfying (R1)–(R4) is P(x) = \|ψ(x)\|², with reality + non-negativity + phase-invariance + bilinearity forcing the form uniquely

**Theorem 7.2 (Born rule from dx₄/dt = ic).** *Let ψ: ℝ³ → ℂ be the McGucken wavefunction of Definition 2.6, normalized so that ∫*ℝ³ \|ψ\|² d³x = 1. The unique density P: ℝ³ → ℝ*{≥0} satisfying (R1)–(R4) is*

$$P(\mathbf{x}) = |\psi(\mathbf{x})|^2.$$

*Proof.* By (R4), P is bilinear in (ψ, ψ\*). The general bilinear form is

P(ψ) = a ψψ + b ψ\^\* ψ + c ψ ψ\^\* + d ψ^\* ψ^\* = a ψ² + (b + c) ψ\^\* ψ + d (ψ\^\*)²,

with coefficients a, b, c, d ∈ ℂ.

*Phase invariance fixes the cross-term structure.* By (R3), P(e\^iα ψ) = P(ψ) for all α ∈ ℝ. Under ψ → e\^iα ψ, ψ\^\* → e\^-iα ψ\^*, the terms transform as: ψ² → e\^2iα ψ², ψ\^* ψ → ψ\^\* ψ, (ψ\^*)² → e\^-2iα (ψ\^*)². Phase invariance for all α forces a = d = 0, leaving

P(ψ) = C ψ\^\* ψ, with C := b + c.

*Reality fixes C to be real.* By (R1), P ∈ ℝ. Since ψ\* ψ = \|ψ\|² ∈ ℝ\_{≥0}, C must be real.

*Non-negativity fixes C ≥ 0.* By (R2), P ≥ 0. Since ψ\* ψ ≥ 0, C ≥ 0.

*Normalization fixes C = 1.* The case C = 0 gives P ≡ 0, excluded by the requirement that P be a probability density. Hence C \> 0. The normalization ∫ \|ψ\|² d³x = 1 then fixes C = 1, giving

$$P(\mathbf{x}) = |\psi(\mathbf{x})|^2. \qquad \blacksquare$$

*Status note (form of the Born rule derived).* Theorem 7.2 derives the *projective* form of the Born rule P = \|ψ\|² on the McGucken-derived Hilbert space 𝓗 — the form Born stated in 1926, the form in every textbook, and the form that the Dirac–von Neumann measurement axiom (Corollary 11.3) instantiates. The POVM generalization (Davies–Lewis 1970; Neumaier 2025; see §7.1.16) extends the projective form to real quantum measurements with finite efficiency, losses, dark counts, and simultaneous position-momentum content. The POVM rule is recoverable in the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework via Naimark dilation: any POVM on 𝓗 lifts to a projection-valued measure on 𝓗 ⊗ 𝒦 for an ancilla space 𝒦, and Theorem 7.2 applies on the dilated space, reproducing the POVM rule on 𝓗. The architectural inversion of the present derivation — from postulated rule to forced theorem of dx₄/dt = ic — carries to the POVM form by this dilation.

*Extended status note (the exponent 2 reinforced through the Hilbert-space derivation route).* The exponent 2 in the Born rule P = \|ψ\|² is derived in Lemma 7.1 and Theorem 7.2 from the rank-2 character of the Minkowski metric on the constraint surface Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$, with the rank-2 character itself a forced consequence of $(ic)^2 = -c^2$ via Lemma 2.5. This is the primary route. A second route to the same exponent, derivationally disjoint from the rank-2-metric route, descends from the Hilbert space itself — which is derived from dx₄/dt = ic in Theorem 6.1 — through the parallelogram identity established in Lemma 7.6 as a McGucken-internal consequence of rank-2 sesquilinearity, then through L²-norm conservation under the McGucken-derived unitary evolution of Theorem 9.2.

The McGucken-derived Hilbert space 𝓗 ≅ L²(ℝ³, d³x) of Theorem 6.1 is the Cauchy completion of the space of complex-valued square-integrable amplitudes on the spatial slice, with the L² norm supplied by the inner product induced by the geometric overlap of forward and conjugate x₄-expansions. By Lemma 7.6 (McGucken-internal), the parallelogram identity

‖x + y‖² + ‖x − y‖² = 2(‖x‖² + ‖y‖²)

holds as a direct two-line algebraic consequence of the rank-2 sesquilinearity of the inner product supplied by Lemma 7.1 — without invoking any external functional-analytic theorem. The rank-2 sesquilinearity descends from (ict)² = −c² t² (Lemma 2.5), which is the squared form of dx₄/dt = ic. The L²-norm structure of 𝓗 is therefore a direct consequence of the rank-2 metric, internal to the dx₄/dt = ic framework.

A further reinforcement of the exponent 2 comes from unitarity. Theorem 9.2 establishes that the McGucken-derived Schrödinger evolution preserves the L² norm exactly:

(d/dt) ∫\_ℝ³ \|ψ(x, t)\|² d³x = 0.

For p ≠ 2 the L\^p norm of a normalized solution to the Schrödinger equation is not in general preserved by unitary evolution; the proof is by direct computation. For a normalized 3D Gaussian wavepacket with spatial width σ(t) \~ ℏt/(2mσ_0) at large t, the L\^p norm scales as ‖ψ_t‖\_p \~ σ(t)\^{3(2-p)/(2p)} \~ t\^{-3(p-2)/(2p)} for p \> 2 (verification: at p = 4 the L\^p norm decays as t\^{-3/4}, since ∫\|ψ_t\|⁴ d³x \~ σ(t)\^{-3} and σ(t)\^{-3/4} \~ t\^{-3/4}). For p \< 2 the exponent 3(2-p)/(2p) is positive and the L\^p norm grows as a positive power of t — non-conserved in the opposite direction. Only p = 2 makes the exponent vanish, conserving the norm exactly. Lesovik (G. B. Lesovik, “Derivation of the Born rule from the unitarity of quantum evolution,” arXiv:1411.6992, 2014; \[124\]) gives the explicit derivation of the Born rule’s exponent 2 from precisely this unitarity argument on a given Hilbert space. In the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework, Lesovik’s argument applies on the *derived* Hilbert space 𝓗 of Theorem 6.1, with the unitary evolution itself derived in Theorem 9.2, and the parallelogram-identity / inner-product structure of 𝓗 supplied internally by Lemma 7.6. The exponent 2 is therefore forced from the dynamical side as well: probability conservation under the unitary evolution of Theorem 9.2, which descends from dx₄/dt = ic, requires the bilinear L² norm whose existence on 𝓗 is internal to the dx₄/dt = ic framework via Lemma 7.6.

The exponent 2 in the Born rule is therefore *overdetermined* by two derivationally disjoint McGucken-internal routes that share no intermediate machinery between the McGucken Principle and the conclusion:

*Metric Route (rank-2 metric route to bilinear density).* dx₄/dt = ic → Lorentzian metric on Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ (Lemma 2.5) → rank-2 character of g_μν → natural bilinear pairing on (ψ, ψ\*) (Lemma 7.1) → P = \|ψ\|² (Theorem 7.2). Geometric machinery: metric tensor, rank counting, sesquilinear pairing on amplitudes.

*Norm Route (rank-2 sesquilinear inner product route to L²-norm structure, McGucken-internal).* dx₄/dt = ic → Lorentzian metric on Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ (Lemma 2.5) → rank-2 sesquilinear inner product on 𝓥 (Lemma 7.1) → parallelogram identity by direct two-line expansion (Lemma 7.6) → L²-norm structure on the McGucken-derived 𝓗 (Theorem 6.1); reinforced by unitarity (Theorem 9.2) preserving the L² norm exactly. Functional-analytic machinery: rank-2 sesquilinearity, parallelogram identity, Stone’s theorem on unitary groups, L\^p norm-conservation analysis — all internal to the dx₄/dt = ic framework via Lemma 7.6.

Both routes start from dx₄/dt = ic; both routes end at P = \|ψ\|²; they share only the upstream principle and the rank-2 → sesquilinear chain (Lemma 2.5 → Lemma 7.1) before diverging. Metric Route operates through the density’s degree directly (rank-2 bilinear pairing → quadratic density). Norm Route operates through the norm structure and conservation (rank-2 sesquilinearity → parallelogram identity → L² norm → unitarity conservation). The two routes converge on the same exponent through entirely different mathematical structure, both descending from the same upstream physical principle, both internal to the dx₄/dt = ic framework.

*Status of Jordan–von Neumann 1935 in the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework.* The Jordan–von Neumann theorem \[123\] historically established that a normed space admits an inner product if and only if its norm satisfies the parallelogram identity, with the corollary that among L\^p spaces only L² is a Hilbert space. In the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework, this theorem is *unnecessary as upstream input*: the inner product on 𝓗 is supplied directly by Lemma 7.1 from the rank-2 Minkowski metric, and the parallelogram identity follows by Lemma 7.6 as a McGucken-internal downstream consequence. Jordan–von Neumann therefore serves as a *downstream consistency check* — confirming that the McGucken-derived parallelogram-identity structure on the McGucken-derived 𝓗 is consistent with general functional analysis on L\^p spaces — rather than as a foundational selection principle. The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework derives the L² character of 𝓗 internally; Jordan–von Neumann’s historical theorem is cited as the standard functional-analytic correlate but is no longer used as upstream input to the cascade.

The architectural significance of this overdetermination is derivational: *no prior program in the foundations of quantum mechanics derived the Hilbert space from a physical principle upstream of the formalism, and none derived the parallelogram identity from a physical principle internal to the dx₄/dt = ic framework.* Gleason (1957) derived the form of the Born rule on a *given* Hilbert space; the trace structure on the lattice of subspaces already encodes the inner-product-derived bilinearity. Jordan–von Neumann (1935) characterized the parallelogram identity on *given* L\^p spaces; the result is a theorem about which Banach spaces admit inner products, with the L\^p spaces themselves taken as input. Lesovik (2014) derived the Born rule from unitarity on a *given* Hilbert space; the Hilbert space hosting the unitary evolution is presupposed. Each of these results, in the orthodox tradition, takes the Hilbert space or the inner product as input and derives the exponent 2 from inside that input.

The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework operates one level upstream of all three programs: the Hilbert space itself is derived (Theorem 6.1) from dx₄/dt = ic, the inner product is supplied internally (Lemma 7.1) from the rank-2 metric, the parallelogram identity is internal to the dx₄/dt = ic framework (Lemma 7.6) by direct two-line algebra, and the orthodox inside-Hilbert-space arguments — Gleason, Jordan–von Neumann, Lesovik — all reinforce the exponent 2 *with their inputs themselves traced back to dx₄/dt = ic*. The exponent 2 has, in the McGucken framework, multiple internally-consistent derivations all descending from the same physical principle, with the Hilbert space as derived intermediate, the inner product as derived sesquilinear pairing, and the parallelogram identity as derived McGucken-internal algebraic consequence — rather than as primitive inputs. This is the *exponent-2 overdetermination property* of the dx₄/dt = ic framework: every functional-analytic argument that forces the exponent on a given Hilbert space (Jordan–von Neumann uniqueness, Lesovik unitarity, Gleason non-contextuality) is, in the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework, an argument whose Hilbert-space input and inner-product input are themselves theorems of dx₄/dt = ic — so each functional-analytic route to the exponent ultimately traces back to the same upstream principle as the geometric rank-2-metric route, and the parallelogram-identity step internal to Norm Route is itself a McGucken-internal consequence of rank-2 sesquilinearity (Lemma 7.6), not an external functional-analytic input.

### 7.6 Exclusion of alternative Born-density candidates: \|ψ\|\^p for p ≠ 2 fails phase invariance + bilinearity; ψ·ψ fails reality; Re(ψ) fails phase invariance; the (R1)–(R4) requirements force \|ψ\|² uniquely

Theorem 7.2’s uniqueness argument rules out the alternative densities that have appeared in proposals over the past century:

-   **P = \|ψ\| is excluded by (R4).** The modulus \|ψ\| = √(ψ\* ψ) is the square root of a bilinear in (ψ, ψ\*). Geometrically the projection of forward x₄-advance onto its conjugate has degree two, not one.
-   **P = \|ψ\|³ is excluded by (R4).** Not bilinear. Geometrically there is no 1.5-fold conjugation of x₄.
-   **P = ψ² is excluded by (R1) and (R3).** Complex-valued in general; not phase-invariant under ψ → e\^{iα} ψ.

The rule P = \|ψ\|² is the density that bilinearity, phase invariance, reality, and non-negativity force, given the geometry of dx₄/dt = ic.

  \## 7.7.2 How Born arrived at the rule: the historical   canvas against which the geo     metric derivation is set                         

  e claim that the framework *derives* what Born \*posit   ed\* requires an accurate acco   unt of how Born arrived at the rule, since th    e force of the claim depends on what was and was not established in 1926. The historical record is documented in Born’s 1926 paper (Born 1926, ref. \[212\]), his 1954 Nobel lecture, and the century of history-of-physics scholarship since (Landsman, “The Born rule and its interpretation”; the centenary review “The Born rule — 100 years ago and today,” arXiv:2502.08545). It shows that Born reached $|\psi|^2$ by physical analogy and empirical adequacy, and never by derivation from a principle — which is the precise sense in which “why the square?” remained an open question for a century.

  he problem Born was attacking.\* In mid-1926, immediat   ely after Schrödinger’s wave     mechanics appeared, Born applied it to electr    on–atom scattering. Schrödinger read $\psi$ realistically: the wave packet was the electron, $\psi$ a real charge or matter distribution spread through space. Born found this could not survive the collision problem: after scattering, the wave spreads as an outgoing spherical wave in all directions, yet experiment registers a whole electron arriving at one definite place on the detector. A smeared distribution cannot do this. Born concluded that Schrödinger’s mathematics was correct and his physical interpretation wrong, and in the 1926 paper wrote that quantum mechanics answers not “what is the state after the collision” but only “how probable is a given effect of the collision,” adding that “there is no quantity that in an individual case fixes the effect of the collision.” This is the introduction of fundamental indeterminism: Born relinquished the question of where the electron goes and kept only the probability.

  hat motivated the idea: Einstein’s ghost field.\* Born   was explicit, in his 1954 No     bel lecture, that the idea came from Einstein    : “Again an idea of Einstein’s gave me the lead. He had tried to make the duality of particles — light quanta or photons — and waves comprehensible by interpreting the square of the optical wave amplitudes as probability density for the occurrence of photons. This concept could at once be carried over to the $\psi$-function.” The model was Einstein’s “ghost field” (Gespensterfeld): a guiding field carrying no energy that sets where the photon is likely to be found. Born took $\psi$ as the ghost field of de Broglie’s electron — $\psi$ does not locate the electron, it sets the probability of finding it. The motivating problem was wave–particle duality: how a spread-out wave and a localized particle can be one thing, resolved by having the wave govern the probability and the particle be what is detected.

  hy the square, and the footnote added in proof.\* The    origin of the exponent is pre    cise and documented. In the main text of the     1926 paper Born first wrote that $\psi$ itself — the amplitude — gives the probability (*“$\psi$ bestimmt die Wahrscheinlichkeit”*). In a footnote added in proof, after submission, he corrected it: the probability is proportional to $|\psi|^2$, the square of the modulus. The most consequential relation in quantum mechanics, $P = |\psi|^2$, thus entered physics as a hand-corrected footnote, and Born himself did not initially distinguish $\psi$ from $|\psi|^2$ until he fixed it in proof. The square was reached by two converging analogies, neither a derivation. First, the optics analogy: in classical wave optics the intensity — the physically measurable energy density — is the square of the wave amplitude, and Einstein’s ghost-field move read this squared optical amplitude as photon probability density; Born carried it directly to $\psi$, inheriting the square from the fact that energy in any wave theory goes as amplitude squared. Second, two consistency requirements that only the square satisfies: $\psi$ is complex, so $\psi$ itself cannot be a probability, while $|\psi|^2 = \psi^*\psi$ is real and non-negative; and only the squared modulus gives a conserved, normalizable total probability, $\int |\psi|^2 d^3x = 1$ preserved under the evolution through the continuity equation. Born recognized after the fact that the square was the only quantity that could serve as a probability; he did not derive that it must be the square.

  he documented verdict.\* The history-of-physics litera   ture is uniform: Born reached    the rule by analogy to optical intensity, co     rrected the amplitude-versus-square question in a footnote, and justified the result by its success in scattering, not by a principle. Born himself, the scholarship records, did not attempt to motivate the rule theoretically but appealed to experimental confirmation. This is why “why the square?” stands as a genuine open question of foundations rather than a settled matter: the exponent 2 was borrowed from classical wave-intensity and forced consistency-wise by the complex character of $\psi$ and by probability conservation, but never grounded in a physical reason for the squaring itself.

  he framework against this canvas.\* The McGucken deriv   ation supplies the physical r    eason Born’s construction lacked, and it does    so in the same element Born reached for. Born’s square came from wave intensity — amplitude squared — which is a property of a spherical wavefront; the framework identifies the wavefront as the physical McGucken Sphere and derives the exponent 2 from its geometry: the rank-2 character of the metric forcing bilinearity in $(\psi, \psi^*)$ (Lemma 7.1), the parallelogram identity of the inner-product norm (Lemma 7.6), and the unitarity of the derived evolution excluding every $p \neq 2$ (Theorem 9.2, §7.5–7.6), with the measure fixed as the unique SO(3)-invariant measure on the Sphere (Theorem 7.2, Lemma 7.1.5). The two analogies Born used are, in the framework, two faces of one derived fact: the intensity-equals-amplitude-squared of wave optics is the Huygens-wavefront intensity of the expanding McGucken Sphere (§4.3), and the consistency requirements Born noted — complex $\psi$, conserved $|\psi|^2$ — are the phase-invariance and unitarity that the same Sphere geometry enforces. Born inherited the square from the optics of intensity and could not say why; the framework derives it from the geometry of the expanding wavefront, and identifies Born’s own motivating analogy — the squared amplitude of a spherical wave — as the physics of dx₄/dt = ic. The century-old “why the square” is answered not by overturning Born’s route but by grounding the wave-intensity analogy he followed in the physical sphere whose invariant measure the square is.
