## 11. The five Dirac–von Neumann axioms (states as unit vectors, observables as self-adjoint operators, Born rule, projection postulate, unitary Schrödinger dynamics) as corollaries of the cogenerative cascade — Corollaries 11.1–11.6 — immediate consequences of the upstream theorems rather than primitive postulates

The orthodox foundation of quantum mechanics, synthesized from Dirac’s 1930 *Principles of Quantum Mechanics* and von Neumann’s 1932 *Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik*, consists of five axioms (sometimes called postulates) that have served for nearly a century as the starting point of the theory. This section establishes that all five Dirac–von Neumann axioms are *corollaries* of theorems already proved in the McGucken cascade — immediate downstream consequences of the upstream theorems §§2–9.

### 11.1 Theorems and corollaries in the cascade — a methodological note

A theorem in this paper does derivational work: it advances the cascade by establishing a new structure or relation from prior structures. Theorem 2.4 establishes 𝓜_G; Lemma 2.5 establishes Minkowski space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$; Theorem 3.1 establishes complex amplitudes; Theorem 5.1 establishes the canonical commutator; Theorem 6.1 establishes the Hilbert space; Theorem 7.2 establishes the Born rule; Theorem 8.2 establishes the uncertainty bound; Theorem 9.1 establishes the Schrödinger equation; Theorem 9.2 establishes unitarity. Each is a step in the chain.

The five Dirac–von Neumann axioms, by contrast, do no new derivational work in the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework. They are textbook *re-packagings* of theorems already established. The Hilbert-space axiom (Dirac–von Neumann axiom 1) is the abstract textbook formulation of Theorem 6.1. The self-adjoint-operator axiom (Dirac–von Neumann axiom 2) is the operator-language re-statement of the conservation requirement underlying Theorem 9.2. The Born axiom (Dirac–von Neumann axiom 3) is the operator-eigenvector re-statement of Theorem 7.2. The projection axiom (Dirac–von Neumann axiom 4) is the textbook re-statement of Theorem 7.4’s geometric reading of measurement. The Schrödinger axiom (Dirac–von Neumann axiom 5) is the textbook statement of Theorem 9.1.

**The McGucken derivation of the Dirac–von Neumann corollaries from a deeper foundational principle is the feature that distinguishes this paper from every prior reconstruction attempt — including the most recent and most sophisticated.** Hardy (2001), Chiribella–D’Ariano–Perinotti (2011), Masanes–Müller (2011–2019), Höhn (2017), and Barandes (2023, 2025) each reconstruct the Dirac–von Neumann formalism (or an empirically equivalent reformulation of it) from operational, informational, or stochastic axioms — but in each case the reconstruction trades the orthodox postulates for a different set of postulates whose physical origin is itself unexplained. Hardy’s five operational axioms, Chiribella–D’Ariano–Perinotti’s purification postulate, Masanes–Müller’s state-space dimension axioms, Höhn’s information-acquisition rules, and Barandes’s indivisibility axiom are each *as foundational as* the Dirac–von Neumann axioms they replace; each is a sideways move from one set of primitive assumptions to another, not an upstream move to a single physical principle from which all primitive assumptions descend.

The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework is different. The five Dirac–von Neumann statements are not replaced by an alternative axiomatic system; they are *derived* — together with the structures they make statements about — from a single physical principle: dx₄/dt = ic, with action ℏ per Planck-frequency oscillation of x₄-advance. Every Dirac–von Neumann corollary in §§11.2–11.7 traces upstream through the cascade to this one principle: Corollary 11.1 (state axiom) traces through Theorem 6.1 to the cascade dx₄/dt = ic → Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ → 𝓥 → 𝓗; Corollary 11.2 (observable axiom) traces through Theorem 9.2 (x₄-flux conservation, unitarity) and Stone’s theorem; Corollary 11.3 (Born rule) traces through Theorem 7.2 to the rank-2 character of the Minkowski metric and the universality of x₄-expansion; Corollary 11.4 (collapse) traces through Theorem 7.4 to the geometric incidence of forward and conjugate x₄-expansions at the apparatus; Corollary 11.5 (Schrödinger dynamics) traces through Theorems 9.1 and 9.2 to the perpendicularity-and-action-quantization structure of x₄-advance; and Corollary 11.6 (composite-system tensor product) traces through Theorem 6.1 and Fubini–Tonelli to the universality of x₄-expansion from independent events.

This is the architectural inversion in its sharpest form. Every other reconstruction in the foundations literature replaces the Dirac–von Neumann axioms with a different set of axioms (operational, informational, stochastic, categorical) and then derives a structure empirically equivalent to QM from those replacement axioms. The replacement axioms become the new foundation. The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework eliminates the layer of foundation-by-postulation altogether: there are no replacement axioms, only one physical principle, with everything else — the Hilbert space, the observables, the Born rule, the collapse rule, the Schrödinger evolution, the tensor-product structure — derived as forced consequences. The Dirac–von Neumann statements appear as corollaries (downstream consequences) rather than as theorems (derivational theorems) because they descend from the McGucken Principle. They are the standard quantum-mechanical statements seen as immediate consequences of the deeper derivations in the cascade, with the deeper foundational principle (dx₄/dt = ic) being the only foundational assumption.

This is the methodological reason the Dirac–von Neumann statements are presented as corollaries, not theorems: they are immediate consequences of upstream theorems. There is also a reason. A foundational derivation is more impressive when the textbook axioms appear as corollaries of upstream theorems than when they appear as side-by-side theorems. The cascade structure — dx₄/dt = ic → Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ → 𝓥 → 𝓗 → Born/CCR/uncertainty/Schrödinger → Dirac–von Neumann corollaries — makes the architectural inversion visible: what the orthodox tradition posited as five primitive axioms appear at the bottom of the cascade as automatic consequences of one physical principle.

*Identification with the McGucken Quantum Formalism.* In the language of the McGucken Quantum Formalism \[114\], the five Dirac–von Neumann statements correspond to the four conditions (Q1)–(Q4) of its quantum layer (\[114, Definition 9.1\]): (Q1) the Hilbert space (Dirac–von Neumann axiom 1, Corollary 11.1), (Q2) the self-adjoint operator algebra with \[q̂, p̂\] = iℏ (Dirac–von Neumann axiom 2, Corollary 11.2), (Q3) the Schrödinger wave-function evolution (Dirac–von Neumann axiom 5, Corollary 11.5), and the Born-projection content (Dirac–von Neumann axiom 3 and Dirac–von Neumann axiom 4, Corollaries 11.3 and 11.4) is the measurement-side consequence of the dual-channel pairing of forward and conjugate x₄-expansions in (Q4). The McGucken Quantum Formalism’s dual-channel sextuple (M, F, V; H, A, ψ) of \[114, Definition 9.2\] is therefore their *foundational derivation*: the sextuple is what the postulates point at when read as corollaries of dx₄/dt = ic rather than as primitive axioms.

The five corollaries are now stated and proved.

### 11.2 Corollary Dirac–von Neumann axiom 1: States as unit vectors in a complex separable Hilbert space

**Corollary 11.1 (Dirac–von Neumann state axiom from Theorem 6.1).** *The state of a quantum system is represented by a unit vector ψ in a complex separable Hilbert space 𝓗, defined up to overall phase. Equivalently, pure states are rays in 𝓗, and general states are density operators ρ with tr(ρ) = 1 and ρ ≥ 0.*

*Proof.* By Theorem 6.1, 𝓗 ≅ L²(Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$, dμ_M) is the Cauchy completion of the pre-Hilbert space of complex-valued square-integrable amplitudes over the McGucken-derived Lorentzian spacetime. The McGucken wavefunction ψ (Definition 2.6) is a point in this space.

*Normalization.* The Born probability density (Theorem 7.2) is P = \|ψ\|², and the requirement that total probability sum to unity gives

∫\_ℝ³ \|ψ(x, t)\|² d³x = 1,

which is the statement that ψ is a *unit* vector in 𝓗 with respect to the McGucken-derived inner product.

*Phase invariance.* By requirement (R3) in the Born derivation (§7.3), the Born density is invariant under global phase ψ → e\^iαψ for all α ∈ ℝ. Geometrically, this is the universality of the x₄-expansion from every event: a homogeneous shift of the x₄-origin is unobservable. Two unit vectors differing by an overall phase therefore represent the same physical state. The set of physical states is the projective Hilbert space ℙ𝓗 = (𝓗 ∖ {0})/\~ where ψ \~ e\^{iα} ψ for any α ∈ ℝ — i.e., the set of *rays* in 𝓗 (nonzero vectors quotiented by the U(1) phase-equivalence relation).

*Density operators.* For statistical mixtures, the natural extension is to convex combinations of pure-state projectors: ρ = ∑\_i p_i \|ψ_i⟩⟨ψ_i\| with p_i ≥ 0 and ∑\_i p_i = 1. This forces tr(ρ) = 1, ρ ≥ 0, and ρ = ρ\^† — the standard density-operator axioms — as automatic consequences of the convex-combination structure on the derived 𝓗.

*Separability.* The McGucken-derived 𝓗 is L²(Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$, dμ_M), which is separable because Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ as a constraint surface in E₄ carries a σ-finite measure Σ_M inherited from Lebesgue measure on ℝ³ and the proper-time measure. L² spaces of separable measure spaces are separable Hilbert spaces by the Riesz–Fischer theorem and the existence of countable dense subsets in L². ∎

The Dirac–von Neumann state axiom is therefore not an independent assertion. It is the statement that the McGucken-derived 𝓗 from Theorem 6.1 has the standard textbook properties of a complex separable Hilbert space, with normalized vectors representing states up to phase. Every element of the axiom is forced by Theorem 6.1 plus the Born rule (Theorem 7.2) plus the universality clause of dx₄/dt = ic.

### 11.3 Corollary Dirac–von Neumann axiom 2: Observables as self-adjoint operators

**Corollary 11.2 (Dirac–von Neumann observable axiom from Theorems 5.1, 8.2).** *Physical observables are self-adjoint operators on the McGucken-derived Hilbert space 𝓗. The spectrum of a self-adjoint operator gives the possible measurement outcomes.*

*Proof.* An observable Â on 𝓗 represents a measurable physical quantity. Two requirements force self-adjointness.

*Real-valued spectrum.* Physical measurements yield real numbers. The expectation value ⟨ Â ⟩ = ⟨ψ\|Â\|ψ⟩ must be real for every ψ ∈ 𝓗. The standard linear-algebraic fact is that ⟨ψ\|Â\|ψ⟩ ∈ ℝ for all ψ if and only if Â is self-adjoint: Â = Â\^†. The spectral theorem on a complex separable Hilbert space then guarantees that the spectrum of a self-adjoint Â is a subset of ℝ, and that Â admits a spectral decomposition Â = ∫ λ dP_λ where the P_λ are spectral projectors. The eigenvalues of Â (more precisely, points in its spectrum) are the possible measurement outcomes.

The conjunction of the two arguments — real-valued spectra from measurement, self-adjoint generators from unitarity — fixes the observable status as self-adjoint operators on the derived 𝓗. ∎

### 11.4 Corollary Dirac–von Neumann axiom 3: The Born rule

**Corollary 11.3 (Dirac–von Neumann measurement axiom from Theorem 7.2).** \*Let Â be a self-adjoint observable with spectral decomposition Â = ∑\_n a_n \|a_n⟩⟨ a_n\| (for the discrete case; the continuous case extends analogously via the spectral measure). ### 11.6 Corollary Dirac–von Neumann axiom 5: Unitary Schrödinger evolution

**Corollary 11.5 (Dirac–von Neumann dynamics axiom from Theorems 9.1, 9.2).** *Between measurements, the state ψ evolves unitarily according to the Schrödinger equation*

*Proof.* Theorem 9.1 establishes the Schrödinger equation as the unique first-order linear evolution along x₄ generated by the McGucken source operator on the derived Hilbert space, with both factors of iℏ on the left descending from the McGucken Principle’s twin constants (i from perpendicularity of x₄, ℏ from action quantization of x₄-advance). The evolution operator solving iℏ ∂\_t ψ = Ĥ ψ with initial condition ψ(0) is ψ(t) = U(t) ψ(0) where

U(t) = exp(-iĤ t/ℏ).

By Theorem 9.2, U(t) preserves the inner product: ⟨ U(t)ψ \| U(t)φ ⟩ = ⟨ψ\|φ⟩ for all ψ, φ ∈ 𝓗 and all t ∈ ℝ. An inner-product-preserving bijection of a Hilbert space is unitary by definition; equivalently, U\^† U = U U\^† = I. By Stone’s theorem, every one-parameter unitary group U(t) on a complex Hilbert space is of the form U(t) = e\^-iÂ t/ℏ for a unique self-adjoint generator Â, and conversely every self-adjoint Â generates such a group. Taking Â = Ĥ recovers the standard Schrödinger dynamics.

Hence: iℏ ∂\_t ψ = Ĥ ψ as the differential form, with U(t) = e\^-iĤ t/ℏ as the unitary evolution operator, both immediate from Theorems 9.1 and 9.2. ∎

The Dirac–von Neumann dynamics axiom is therefore Theorem 9.1 plus Theorem 9.2 in textbook language. The differential form is Theorem 9.1; the unitary form is Theorem 9.2 via Stone’s theorem. No new derivational content.

### 11.7 The composite-system axiom (Dirac–von Neumann axiom 6)

A sixth axiom is sometimes added to the Dirac–von Neumann list: the Hilbert space of a composite system AB is the tensor product 𝓗_AB = 𝓗_A ⊗ 𝓗_B.

**Corollary 11.6 (Composite-system axiom from Theorem 6.1).** *For two independent subsystems A and B with derived Hilbert spaces 𝓗_A = L²(M⁽ᴬ⁾₁,₃, dμ_M) and 𝓗_B = L²(M⁽ᴮ⁾₁,₃, dμ_M), the combined system’s Hilbert space is the tensor product*

𝓗_AB = 𝓗_A ⊗ 𝓗_B ≅ L²(M⁽ᴬ⁾₁,₃ × M⁽ᴮ⁾₁,₃, dμ_M\^(A) ⊗ dμ_M\^(B)).

*Proof.* By Theorem 6.1, each subsystem’s Hilbert space is the L² completion of complex amplitudes over its constraint surface. The constraint surface of the composite system is the Cartesian product M⁽ᴬ⁾₁,₃ × M⁽ᴮ⁾₁,₃ — each subsystem carrying its own copy of x₄-expansion from its own events. The natural measure on the product is the product measure dμ_M\^(A) ⊗ dμ_M\^(B). The Fubini–Tonelli theorem then gives

L²(M⁽ᴬ⁾₁,₃ × M⁽ᴮ⁾₁,₃, dμ\^(A)\_M ⊗ dμ\^(B)\_M) ≅ L²(M⁽ᴬ⁾₁,₃, dμ\^(A)\_M) ⊗ L²(M⁽ᴮ⁾₁,₃, dμ\^(B)\_M) = 𝓗_A ⊗ 𝓗_B. ∎

The tensor-product structure for composite systems is therefore an immediate corollary of Theorem 6.1 applied to product measure spaces. The Fubini–Tonelli theorem is standard real analysis; the only physical input is the recognition that two independent subsystems carry two independent constraint surfaces, which is the statement that x₄-expansion from event E_A is independent of x₄-expansion from event E_B — the universality clause of dx₄/dt = ic applied to two events.

## 12. Measurement as physical Wick rotation (Theorem 12.2): the measurement event physically realizes the rotation removing the i-marker for x₄-perpendicularity from the particle’s amplitude, with the same geometric effect as the formal Wick rotation in path-integral QFT; statistical-cumulative version (Theorem 12.4) and the universal non-closure quantum (Theorem 12.11 across nine instances of foundational physics)

The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework identifies a single geometric operation that runs through the cascade at multiple levels: the squaring that removes the perpendicularity-marker i from an i-bearing x₄-perpendicular structure, producing a real-valued spatial-slice quantity. At the kinematic level, this squaring is what takes the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic to the Lorentzian metric ds² = −c²dt² + dx²_spatial: the operation (ic)² = −c² removes the i, with the resulting −c² appearing as the temporal component of the rank-2 invariant (Lemma 2.5). This section identifies the physical event at which the amplitude-level squaring occurs: the moment of measurement. ### 12.1 The dual squaring: kinematic and amplitude levels of the same operation

The squaring at the kinematic level is Lemma 2.5: the Lorentzian signature (−, +, +, +) of the Minkowski metric is forced by (ict)² = −c² t², which is dx₄/dt = ic squared with time. The metric is the rank-2, real-valued, non-chiral invariant that one obtains by squaring the rank-1, i-bearing, perpendicular principle dx₄/dt = ic. The squaring at the amplitude level is Theorem 7.4 with Lemma 7.1: the Born density at a localized absorber’s event is P = \|ψ\|² = ψ\*ψ. The bilinearity is forced by the rank-2 character of the Minkowski metric (Lemma 7.1) — the metric’s rank is inherited by the wavefunction’s inner-product structure, fixing the Born exponent at 2. The same operation that takes the rank-1 dx₄/dt = ic to the rank-2 ds² takes the rank-1 amplitude ψ to the rank-2 density \|ψ\|².

Both squarings are the same geometric operation, applied at two levels of the cascade. Both remove the i that is the perpendicularity-marker for x₄. Both produce a real-valued spatial-slice quantity from an i-bearing x₄-perpendicular structure. The Lorentzian metric is the squared-rate form; the Born density is the squared-amplitude form. The exponent 2 in each is the algebraic signature of the same geometric rotation: from the perpendicular x₄-direction back into the real x₁x₂x₃ directions.

### 12.2 The wavefunction as participation in x₄-expansion

Between measurements, a quantum particle is participating in the x₄-expansion. The particle’s four-velocity u\^μ has a component along x₄, related to its spatial component by the four-velocity budget constraint u\^μ u_μ = −c² (the four-vector form of dx₄/dt = ic; cf. §9.2 step 1). At spatial rest, $d\tau = dt$, and the full four-velocity budget is along x₄: dx₄/dτ = dx₄/dt = ic (rest-frame reading, Lemma 4.7). With spatial motion, the budget is partitioned between spatial and x₄ components, with the total magnitude fixed at c.

The wavefunction ψ on Minkowski space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ is the spatial-slice projection of the particle’s forward x₄-expansion. The complex character of ψ is the imprint of x₄-perpendicularity on its phase. Specifically:

(i) The **phase** of ψ at a spacetime event encodes the particle’s x₄-position contribution at that event. Multiplication by exp(iφ) implements rotation by angle φ in the x₄-perpendicular direction; the phase of ψ at a spatial location is, geometrically, the angle the particle’s x₄-component has accumulated along its worldline to that location.

(ii) The **modulus** \|ψ\| of ψ at a spacetime event encodes the spatial-slice amplitude — the amount of the x₄-expansion that has projected onto that spatial location.

(iii) The **Schrödinger evolution** iℏ ∂\_t ψ = Ĥ ψ (Theorem 9.1, with Theorem 9.2 unitarity) is the chain-rule operator form of dx₄/dt = ic on the constraint surface (Theorem 10.5 clause iv). The i on the left of the Schrödinger equation is the same i as in x₄ = ict — both mark the same perpendicularity.

The wavefunction’s spatial spread between measurements is the geometry of the unbounded spatial reach of x₄-expansion: from any event, the x₄-expansion at c reaches every spatial direction symmetrically, with the spatial-slice projection of this expansion appearing as a wavefunction spreading over space. The nonlocality of ψ is the projection of the x₄-expansion’s locality at the four-dimensional level (the expansion advances at c per proper time, perpendicular to the spatial slice) onto the spatial slice’s three-dimensional geometry (where it appears as instantaneous spatial spread).

### 12.3 The measurement event: rotation out of x₄

**Definition 12.1 (Measurement event).** A *measurement event* is a spacetime event E ∈ Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ at which a quantum particle’s four-velocity is rotated from a configuration with x₄-component (participation in x₄-expansion) to a configuration localized at E (committed to a definite spatial position at a definite t). The geometry of the rotation: the particle’s worldline tangent reorients from the x₄-perpendicular direction toward the spatial directions x₁x₂x₃, removing the x₄-component that was encoded by the wavefunction’s phase.

The mechanism of the rotation is the meeting of two geometric structures at E (Theorem 7.4):

(a) The particle’s **forward x₄-expansion** ψ has amplitude at E. The particle’s wavefunction has reached this spacetime point through its spreading from the emission event, with phase encoding accumulated x₄-component and modulus encoding spatial-slice amplitude.

(b) The detector apparatus has been prepared, by prior decoherence, to register at a definite spatial position. Its **conjugate x₄-image** ψ\* extends back to E, encoding “a localized absorber is here at E, ready to register.” (The conjugate is the same wavefunction with phase reversed — geometrically, the time-reversed/phase-reversed representation of the forward expansion.)

For the rotation out of x₄ to occur at E, both (a) and (b) must be present at E. The probability density that the rotation occurs at E is therefore the bilinear product ψ\*(E) ψ(E), with the exponent 2 recording the count of independent factors that must coincide: the forward expansion arrives at E AND the absorber’s conjugate image extends to E. The squaring is the algebraic signature of the geometric coincidence required for the rotation to take place.

Post-rotation, the particle is localized at E. Its wavefunction has collapsed onto the eigenstate corresponding to detection at E (Corollary 11.4, the projection postulate). The i-bearing participation in x₄-perpendicularity, which the pre-measurement wavefunction encoded in its complex phase, has been removed from the description. The post-measurement state is real-valued in the sense that the i-marker for x₄-perpendicularity is gone — the particle is no longer participating in the spreading x₄-expansion, and the geometry of its description no longer requires the perpendicularity-marker i.

### 12.4 The mathematical Wick rotation as formalization of the physical rotation

The standard mathematical Wick rotation in quantum field theory is the analytic continuation t → −iτ (equivalently, x₄ = ict → x₄\^W := ct), which maps the Lorentzian metric ds² = −c²dt² + dx²_spatial to the Euclidean metric ds_E² = c²dτ² + dx²_spatial. At the path-integral level, the Wick rotation converts oscillating phase weights exp(iS/ℏ) into damped real weights exp(−S_E/ℏ), removing the i from the action.

Geometrically, the Wick rotation removes the i from the Minkowski coordinate x₄ = ict — it rotates x₄ from its imaginary-axis perpendicular direction into a real-axis direction (cf. §4.5 of the present paper; the corpus identifies the Wick rotation as the McGucken-internal coordinate change τ = x₄/c between the integrated form x₄ = ict and the proper-time parameterization, cited at §4.5, §4.4, and the corpus Wick-rotation treatment). The Wick rotation is, in the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework, a coordinate operation that removes the perpendicularity marker, transitioning between the i-bearing description (x₄ perpendicular, dynamics complex) and the i-free description (x₄ real, dynamics Euclidean).

The dx₄/dt = ic framework recognizes the physical measurement event as the *physical* realization of this *mathematical* rotation. The mathematical Wick rotation removes the i from the coordinate x₄. The physical measurement event removes the i from the particle’s description — rotating it out of the x₄-perpendicular direction into a real spatial event. The two are the same geometric operation, performed in different ways: the mathematical operation is performed at the coordinate level via analytic continuation; the physical operation is performed at the particle level via the geometric meeting of forward and conjugate x₄-expansions at a localized absorber.

### 12.5 Theorem 12.2: Measurement as Physical Wick Rotation

**Theorem 12.2 (Measurement as Physical Wick Rotation).** *Let ψ be a wavefunction on Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ representing a quantum particle’s forward x₄-expansion from an emission event. Let E ∈ Minkowski Space $\mathbb{M}_{1,3}$ be a candidate measurement event at which a localized absorber is prepared to register. $$x_4 = ict \;\longrightarrow\; x_4^W := -i x_4 = ct$$
*at the particle’s worldline at E, with the wavefunction’s i-bearing complex amplitude ψ rotated into the real-valued spatial-slice probability density \|ψ(E)\|² = ψ*(E)ψ(E). **Proof.**

(1) The Minkowski coordinate x₄ = ict carries the imaginary unit i as the perpendicularity marker for x₄’s orthogonality to x₁x₂x₃ (Theorem 3.1, §4.3, §4.5). Multiplication by i implements the rotation that takes a spatial direction into the perpendicular x₄-direction.

(2) The Wick rotation x₄ → −ix₄ = ct removes the i from the coordinate. Geometrically, this rotates x₄ from its perpendicular imaginary-axis orientation into the real-axis orientation, mapping the Lorentzian metric ds² = −c²dt² + dx²_spatial to the Euclidean metric ds_E² = c²dτ² + dx²_spatial. This is the standard Wick rotation; in the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework, it is recognized as the coordinate identification between the integrated form x₄ = ict (perpendicular, imaginary axis) and the proper-time parameterization τ = x₄/c (real axis); see §4.5 of the present paper and the corpus Wick-rotation treatment.

(3) Between emission and measurement, the particle’s wavefunction ψ is i-bearing: its complex phase encodes the particle’s accumulated x₄-component along its worldline (Definition 12.1; §12.2 (i)). The wavefunction’s complex character is the imprint of x₄-perpendicularity on its phase, with multiplication by exp(iφ) implementing rotation by angle φ in the perpendicular x₄-direction (Theorem 3.1).

(4) At a measurement event E, the geometric meeting of the forward x₄-expansion ψ with the localized absorber’s conjugate x₄-image ψ\* at E (Theorem 7.4) rotates the particle’s four-velocity out of x₄. The geometric meeting requires both factors to be present at E — the forward expansion’s amplitude AND the conjugate image’s amplitude — with the product ψ\*(E) ψ(E) the algebraic record of the bilinear coincidence (Lemma 7.1, with rank-2 forced by Lemma 2.5).

(5) The product ψ*(E) ψ(E) is real-valued: any complex number z multiplied by its conjugate z* gives \|z\|², a real non-negative quantity. The squaring eliminates the imaginary part of ψ, removing the i that encoded the particle’s participation in x₄-perpendicularity. The result is a real-valued probability density on the spatial slice at E.

(6) The physics of the squaring at the amplitude level is therefore identical to the physics of the Wick rotation at the coordinate level: both remove the i that is the perpendicularity-marker for x₄. The mathematical operation x₄ = ict → ct (Wick rotation at the coordinate level) and the physical operation ψ → \|ψ\|² (squaring at the amplitude level) are the same geometric operation — rotation of the i-bearing perpendicular structure into the real spatial-slice structure — performed at different cascade levels.

(7) The post-measurement state is the particle localized at E, with the wavefunction collapsed onto the corresponding eigenstate (Corollary 11.4). The particle’s worldline tangent has reoriented from the x₄-perpendicular direction toward the spatial directions; it is no longer participating in the spreading x₄-expansion, and its description no longer requires the i-marker for x₄-perpendicularity.

(8) Therefore, the measurement event at E *is* the physical realization of the Wick rotation x₄ → −ix₄, with the i removed at both the coordinate-level (x₄ → ct at the rotation moment) and the amplitude-level (ψ → \|ψ\|² at the rotation moment), with both operations performed in coincidence at the geometric meeting event E. ∎

**Corollary 12.3.** *The standard path-integral Wick rotation, used as a mathematical convergence device in quantum field theory, is the formal abstraction of the physical measurement rotation.* The Wick rotation converts oscillating phase weights exp(iS/ℏ) into damped real weights exp(−S_E/ℏ), removing the i from the path-integral action. The physical measurement event removes the i from the particle’s amplitude, with the same geometric effect: transition from the i-bearing oscillatory description (active x₄-perpendicularity) to the i-free real description (localized spatial event). The Wick rotation has, in the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework, a physical referent: the measurement event in the laboratory.
